metadata.summary: This European guideline addresses the diagnosis, multidisciplinary treatment and follow-up of CNS tumours in children and adolescents. It covers tumour classification, imaging, neurosurgery, neuropathology and radiotherapy, alongside endocrine and visual surveillance and quality of survival. Tumour-specific treatment is addressed in separate sections, while approaches to progression or relapse are outside its stated scope.

conditions_covered: Rare CNS embryonal and sarcomatous tumours
target_population: Children and adolescents diagnosed with a CNS tumour
Children and adolescents undergoing treatment for a CNS tumour
therapeutic_areas: Management of spinal cord compression and cauda equina syndrome

therapies_index.name: watch and wait strategy
approved_indications: Observation without immediate treatment is possible for some CNS tumour types.

therapies_index.name: biopsy
approved_indications: Obtains tissue to establish a CNS tumour diagnosis and identify possible therapeutic targets.
May inform treatment when molecular tumour data are needed.

therapies_index.name: stereotactic biopsy
approved_indications: Provides a tissue diagnosis for brainstem tumours when imaging does not establish a clear diagnosis.

therapies_index.name: endoscopic biopsy
approved_indications: Can establish the pathology of intra- or paraventricular lesions, including pineal tumours with negative tumour markers.
therapies_index.administration: A pineal tumour can be sampled under direct vision through a frontal burr hole.

therapies_index.name: tumour resection
approved_indications: Removes CNS tumour tissue when feasible; its intended extent depends on location and proximity to vital structures.
Can restore CSF circulation when raised intracranial pressure results from tumour obstruction.
therapies_index.administration: The general aim is maximal removal without increasing morbidity or mortality.
key_toxicities: Depending on the structures involved, surgery can produce postoperative visual acuity or visual field deficits and ocular movement abnormalities.
monitoring: Assess resection extent with postoperative MRI rather than CT.

therapies_index.name: gross-total resection
approved_indications: One of the stated surgical objectives for CNS tumours when it can be achieved safely.
monitoring: Determine the postoperative resection extent with MRI.

therapies_index.name: debulking surgery
approved_indications: May relieve spinal cord compression or cauda equina syndrome when removal of the intraspinal mass is feasible.

therapies_index.name: second look procedures
approved_indications: Surgery after neoadjuvant chemotherapy has been beneficial in specific cases, including infants with large tumours in critical locations.

therapies_index.name: CSF drainage
therapies_index.mechanism: Diverts CSF to re-establish its circulation.
approved_indications: A possible surgical approach to raised intracranial pressure caused by disrupted CSF circulation.
therapies_index.administration: An internal or external drain may be used.

therapies_index.name: endoscopic 3rd ventriculostomy
therapies_index.mechanism: Provides a route for CSF circulation.
approved_indications: A possible intervention for raised intracranial pressure associated with impaired CSF flow.

therapies_index.name: endoscopic third ventriculostomy
approved_indications: Can treat obstructive hydrocephalus accompanying a pineal tumour during the same procedure as endoscopic biopsy.

therapies_index.name: decompressive shunt procedures
key_toxicities: Abrupt changes in intracranial pressure after a shunt procedure can interrupt optic nerve blood supply and cause sudden, often irreversible visual acuity or visual field loss.

therapies_index.name: pre-operative embolization
therapies_index.mechanism: Reduces tumour vascularity and alters its consistency to facilitate resection.
approved_indications: May support safer, more complete removal of large vascular tumours, particularly choroid plexus tumours in small children.

therapies_index.name: chemotherapy
approved_indications: Its agents and combinations depend on the CNS tumour entity.
May be part of multimodality treatment for CNS tumours.
key_toxicities: Some chemotherapy agents can cause acute or long-term effects, including visual complications.

therapies_index.name: neoadjuvant chemotherapy
approved_indications: Has preceded beneficial second-look surgery in specific cases, including infants with large tumours in critical locations.
therapies_index.administration: Given before a second-look procedure in the cases described.

therapies_index.name: intrathecal or intraventricular therapy
approved_indications: May be indicated for tumours spreading through the leptomeninges.
therapies_index.administration: Delivered intrathecally or intraventricularly; an Ommaya reservoir is given as an example of intraventricular access.

therapies_index.name: myeloablative chemotherapy with stem cell recue
therapies_index.mechanism: The document suggests that this approach could theoretically increase tumour exposure to cytotoxic drugs.
approved_indications: Used as standard treatment in some protocols and under investigation in ongoing clinical trials.
therapies_index.administration: Myeloablative chemotherapy followed by stem cell rescue; no drug combination or dosing is specified.

therapies_index.name: mTOR inhibitors
approved_indications: The document identifies their use in treating SEGA.

therapies_index.name: BRAF inhibitors
approved_indications: The document identifies their use in low grade glioma.
key_toxicities: Reported ocular effects include uveitis (41%), dry eyes, conjunctivitis and, rarely, photosensitivity (4%).

therapies_index.name: MEK inhibitors
approved_indications: The document identifies their use in low grade glioma.
key_toxicities: Associated retinopathy has been described mainly in adults, from intraretinal fluid detectable only on OCT to retinal vein occlusion with blurred vision and, rarely, irreversible visual acuity loss; whether this retinopathy occurs in children remains unclear.
monitoring: Regular visual acuity assessment and macular OCT/infrared funduscopic imaging may help detect ocular effects and inform treatment interruption or termination.

therapies_index.name: MEK pathway inhibitors
approved_indications: Molecular findings have enabled tailored treatment of some low-grade gliomas with these inhibitors.

therapies_index.name: CCNU
approved_indications: Named among alkylating agents used for selected CNS tumour types.
key_toxicities: The document attributes dose-dependent retinal toxicity to nitrosureas, including CCNU.

therapies_index.name: cisplatin
approved_indications: Named among platinum compounds used for selected CNS tumour types.
key_toxicities: The document attributes dose-dependent retinal toxicity to platinum compounds, including cisplatin.

therapies_index.name: vincristine
approved_indications: Mentioned as an agent used in CNS tumour treatment.
key_toxicities: Rarely reported possible visual toxicity includes unilateral or bilateral ptosis, optic neuropathy and, less frequently, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) and visual loss.

therapies_index.name: methotrexate
approved_indications: Mentioned as an agent used in CNS tumour treatment.
key_toxicities: Rarely reported possible visual toxicity includes unilateral or bilateral ptosis, optic neuropathy and, less frequently, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) and visual loss.

therapies_index.name: steroids
therapies_index.mechanism: High-dose steroids can reduce swelling associated with spinal cord compression or cauda equina syndrome.
approved_indications: An additional treatment option for raised intracranial pressure.
High doses may improve symptoms of spinal cord compression or cauda equina syndrome.
therapies_index.administration: High doses are mentioned for spinal cord compression or cauda equina syndrome; no specific dose or route is given.

therapies_index.name: mannitol
approved_indications: An additional treatment option for raised intracranial pressure.

therapies_index.name: prednisone
key_toxicities: Prolonged exposure is identified as a cataract risk, particularly for prednisone.

therapies_index.name: desmopressin
approved_indications: Generally provides effective management of central diabetes insipidus in children with CNS tumours.
therapies_index.administration: Oral administration is specified; no dose is given.
monitoring: In difficult cases involving disturbed thirst regulation and/or concurrent ACTH deficiency, monitor plasma sodium and fluid intake regularly.

therapies_index.name: GH treatment
approved_indications: Most current recommendations advise that it can be given to brain tumour survivors with established GH deficiency.
Recent guidelines recommend waiting until patients have been disease free for at least one year, while acknowledging that this interval rests on little evidence.

For patients who may never be disease free, such as some with low grade glioma, the possible benefits and harms require individual discussion with the paediatric endocrinologist, oncologist, patient and parents.
therapies_index.administration: The document does not establish an optimal dose.
key_toxicities: Safety regarding recurrence and second tumours has been debated; the cited large cohort studies did not find an increased risk in treated versus untreated childhood cancer survivors, and prospective confirmation is needed.
monitoring: After GH is started, refer to an endocrinologist if FT4 is below the reference interval on 2 separate occasions or falls by > 20 % over time.

therapies_index.name: GnRH analogues
monitoring: Closely monitor pubertal progression after treatment stops in patients with CPP, which may precede LH/ FSHD.

therapies_index.name: radiotherapy
approved_indications: Remains necessary for certain CNS tumour entities despite its toxicity.
Is indicated for low-grade glioma with progression after surgery or when surgery is infeasible, and for all children with high-grade glioma.
Should be considered after resection for patients with ependymoma aged >12 months.
Is part of multimodality treatment for germ cell tumours except completely resected pure mature teratomas.
Is considered after craniopharyngioma surgery according to individual risk.
For rare embryonal tumours and ATRT, its principles generally follow those for medulloblastoma.
Its use for choroid plexus tumours depends on subtype and resection extent.
Is an option for spinal cord compression or cauda equina syndrome when debulking surgery is infeasible and should then begin as soon as possible.
therapies_index.administration: Dose, fractionation, target volumes and technique depend on tumour characteristics and CNS maturity. Treatment may be delayed in children aged less than 12-36 months to limit long-term sequelae.
key_toxicities: Potential acute and long-term effects include neuropsychological deficits.
Cranial exposure can contribute to hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction.
Visual risks include radiation-induced necrosis, retinopathy and amblyopia.
monitoring: Review patients regularly during radiotherapy for support and adverse effects.
Provide risk-adapted long-term surveillance for late effects.

therapies_index.name: craniospinal radiotherapy
approved_indications: All patients with medulloblastoma aged more 3-5 years should be considered for this treatment.

therapies_index.name: Cranio-spinal irradiation (CSI)
approved_indications: Described as routinely used for children with medulloblastoma and other malignant CNS tumours.
key_toxicities: Associated visual effects include dry eye, retinal opacity and posterior subcapsular cataract; these tended to arise at a median time of 27.6 months and occurred in up to 28.8% of children after CSI.
Exposure places children at risk of hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction, primary hypothyroidism, thyroid nodules and thyroid carcinoma.
Spinal irradiation can restrict trunk growth despite adequate GH and sex hormone replacement.
monitoring: Screen thyroid function yearly with TSH and FT4 and perform yearly neck palpation.
Monitor sitting height as well as longitudinal height.

therapies_index.name: IMRT
approved_indications: Named as a technique adopted for CNS tumour radiotherapy.

therapies_index.name: Tomotherapy
approved_indications: Named as a technique adopted for CNS tumour radiotherapy.

therapies_index.name: Proton Beam Therapy
approved_indications: A radiotherapy technique whose option should be discussed by the multidisciplinary team for each child with a CNS tumour; selected patients should be referred in accordance with national clinical guidelines.
key_toxicities: It may reduce adverse effects, particularly late radiotherapy effects, but conclusive evidence from large prospective studies is scarce.
monitoring: Prospective collection of efficacy and toxicity outcomes through national or international protocols is encouraged.

therapies_index.name: particle beam therapy
approved_indications: Selected patients should be referred for this treatment in accordance with national clinical guidelines.

therapies_index.name: highly conformal radiotherapy
approved_indications: Required for patients receiving radiotherapy with curative intent.

therapies_index.name: physiotherapy
approved_indications: Should begin early as part of supportive care for spinal cord compression or cauda equina syndrome.
Access should be available to children with CNS tumours during their care and rehabilitation.

therapies_index.name: occupational therapy
approved_indications: Children and adolescents with CNS tumours should have access to this rehabilitation service.

therapies_index.name: speech therapy
approved_indications: Children and adolescents with CNS tumours should have access to this rehabilitation service.

therapies_index.name: visual impairment rehabilitation
approved_indications: Children with a newly diagnosed CNS tumour and visual signs should be referred to a dedicated service.

therapies_index.name: palliative care
approved_indications: Access should be available as part of care for children and adolescents with CNS tumours.

therapies_index.name: sperm, oocyte or ovarian tissue cryopreservation
approved_indications: Fertility preservation options to consider before gonadotoxic treatment.
therapies_index.administration: Ideally considered before gonadotoxic therapies are administered.

toxicities.incidence: In the St. Jude Lifetime Cohort, 51.4% of adult survivors of childhood cancer treated with cranial RT had at least one anterior pituitary disorder after 27.3 years of follow-up. In a nationwide study of 718 Dutch childhood brain tumour survivors, 22.1% developed at least one endocrine disorder within the first 5 years after diagnosis; the median time at which endocrine disorders appeared was 2.2 years. Among children with medulloblastoma treated with radiation doses of 54 Gy, > 80 % of survivors had HP dysfunction after 5 years of follow-up.
recognition: Possible deficiencies involve GH, TSH, LH/FSH and ACTH.
Risk is increased by younger age at treatment, greater RT dose, suprasellar or sellar tumour location and hydrocephalus.
Dysfunction after radiotherapy can emerge in the 1st year and continue to develop > 10 years after diagnosis.
prevention: Provide endocrine surveillance adapted to treatment exposure and risk.
Refer children with a sellar or suprasellar tumour, or HP dysfunction at diagnosis, directly to a paediatric endocrinologist.

toxicities.incidence: In a study of 3141 CCS with a median follow-up of 24.1 years, GH deficiency prevalence was 22.2%. Among those who received HP radiotherapy, estimated GHD prevalence was 40.2% (n = 1089). In a cohort excluding craniopharyngioma and followed for 6.6 years, growth hormone deficiency occurred in 12.5%. GH deficiency after radiation therapy has been reported as early as 0.1 years.
recognition: A decline in growth trajectory can indicate GH deficiency.
Young age and radiation dose > 18 Gy are listed risk factors in the cranial radiotherapy surveillance table.
Hydrocephalus is associated with greater risk of GH deficiency.
Chemotherapy may temporarily impair statural growth despite adequate GH production; the document states that there is no evidence chemotherapy increases the risk of HP dysfunction.

management.severity: Established GH deficiency in a brain tumour survivor
management.actions: The document reports that most current recommendations support GH administration. It also reports a recent guideline recommendation to wait until the patient has been disease free for at least one year, while noting that evidence for this interval is limited.

management.severity: Persistent disease, including low grade glioma, with GHD
management.actions: The paediatric endocrinologist, oncologist, patient and parents should weigh the potential benefits and harms of GH treatment individually.

prevention: After cranial radiotherapy, measure height, weight, sitting height and BMI every 6 months.

toxicities.event: Other anterior pituitary deficiencies and precocious puberty
toxicities.incidence: In the study of 3141 CCS with a median follow-up of 24.1 years, prevalence was 5.5% for TSH deficiency, 5.1% for LH/FSH deficiency and 4.1% for ACTH deficiency. Among survivors treated with HP radiotherapy, estimated prevalence was 11.1% for TSHD, 10.6% for LH/FSHD, 3.2% for ACTHD and 0.9% for CPP (n = 1089). In the cohort excluding craniopharyngioma followed for 6.6 years, precocious puberty occurred in 12.2%, TSH deficiency in 9.2%, ACTH deficiency in 4.3 % and LH/FSH deficiency in 4.2 %.
recognition: The cranial radiotherapy surveillance table identifies young age and pituitary-region radiation dose > 18 Gy as risk factors for precocious puberty; it identifies pituitary-region radiation dose > 40 Gy for central hypothyroidism, LH/FSH deficiency and ACTH deficiency.
Hydrocephalus may induce central precocious puberty in young children.
CPP may be a risk factor for subsequent LH/ FSHD.

management.severity: FT4 below the reference interval on 2 separate occasions or a decline > 20 % over time after starting GH

prevention: Monitor Tanner stage together with growth velocity every 6 months for the pubertal effects identified after cranial radiotherapy.
Assess TSH and FT4 yearly for central hypothyroidism, and obtain an 08:00 AM morning cortisol yearly when monitoring for ACTH deficiency.
Closely monitor pubertal progression after cessation of GnRH analogues in patients treated for CPP.

toxicities.event: Primary hypothyroidism, thyroid nodules and thyroid carcinoma
recognition: Irradiation involving the thyroid increases the risk of primary hypothyroidism, nodules and thyroid carcinoma.
Combined primary and central hypothyroidism may present with falling FT4 and mildly raised TSH.
The surveillance table lists cervical (stray) irradiation > 20 Gy cranial as a risk factor for thyroidal hypothyroidim and thyroid nodule/ carcinoma.

management.actions: Refer to an endocrinologist for thyroid ultrasound.

prevention: After neck irradiation, including craniospinal irradiation, assess TSH and FT4 and palpate the neck yearly.

Thyroid ultrasound may be considered to surveil for nodules or thyroid cancer; the IGHG advises discussing the method and frequency of surveillance with the patient and parents according to individual needs.

toxicities.incidence: In a nationwide cohort of 661 childhood brain tumour survivors, 33.1% had significant weight gain, overweight, or obesity after a median follow-up of 7.3 years.
recognition: The cohort associated weight gain, overweight or obesity with BMI SDS at diagnosis, low- grade glioma, diabetes insipidus and central precocious puberty.
The cranial radiotherapy surveillance table lists age < 4 years and radiation dose > 20 Gy as risk factors.
prevention: Monitor BMI yearly and provide dietary and physical exercise advice after cranial radiotherapy.

toxicities.event: Reduced spinal growth and short stature
recognition: Spinal irradiation can restrict growth of the back despite adequate GH and sex hormone replacement, particularly during puberty.
prevention: Monitor sitting height as well as longitudinal height; the cervical/spinal radiotherapy surveillance table specifies sitting-height measurement every 6 months.

toxicities.event: Gonadal failure, impaired fertility and pubertal delay or arrest
recognition: Alkylating chemotherapy may cause gonadal failure and delayed or arrested puberty.

In female survivors, possible effects include premature ovarian insufficiency; in male survivors, gonadotoxic treatment may impair spermatogenesis and cause testosterone deficiency or sexual dysfunction.
The document notes that agents considered low-risk may also affect fertility.
prevention: Consider sperm, oocyte or ovarian tissue cryopreservation, ideally before gonadotoxic treatment.
For at-risk female survivors, monitor growth and pubertal development and perform yearly LH/FSH/estradiol monitoring.
Counsel male survivors exposed to alkylating agents or relevant radiation fields about gonadotoxicity; monitor growth and pubertal development in at-risk pre-pubertal and peripubertal survivors.
For postpubertal males, early-morning total serum testosterone testing at clinically appropriate intervals is a reasonable surveillance approach.

recognition: The document describes dose-dependent retinal toxicity with these agents.
Rarely reported possible effects include unilateral or bilateral ptosis and optic neuropathy; posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) and visual loss are described as less frequent.

toxicities.incidence: The document reports uveitis (41%) and photosensitivity in rare cases (4%).
recognition: Reported ocular effects also include dry eyes and conjunctivitis.
Reports, mainly in adults, range from intraretinal fluid visible only on OCT to retinal vein occlusion (RVO), blurred vision and, rarely, irreversible VA loss.
The document states that it is unclear whether MEK-Retinopathy also occurs in children.

management.actions: Regular VA assessment and macular OCT/infrared funduscopic imaging can help guide whether to interrupt or terminate treatment before irreversible visual loss.

prevention: Consider regular VA and macular OCT/infrared funduscopic assessments during MEK inhibitors treatment.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Monitoring can inform a decision to interrupt or terminate treatment before irreversible visual loss; no dose-reduction threshold is specified.

toxicities.incidence: After CSI, dry eye, retinal opacity and posterior subcapsular cataract are reported at a median time of 27.6 months and in up to 28.8% of children. Among patients receiving ≥50 Gy bilaterally to the chiasm or both optic nerves for suprasellar or anterior optic-pathway tumours, between 5% and 8.5% were at risk of VA decline.
recognition: RT-associated visual injury includes radiation-induced necrosis, retinopathy and amblyopia.
Radiation doses (>30Gy) to the posterior fossa or temporal lobes, and prolonged steroid exposure, particularly prednisone, are associated with cataract risk.
An eye dose of 50Gy or more significantly increases the risk of cataracts, double vision, dry eyes and blindness.
Prolonged steroids may cause cataracts.
prevention: Balance the benefit of radiotherapy against its potential late effects when planning treatment.
Consider the radiation tolerance of the lens, optic nerve, optic chiasma, brain stem and cervical medulla.
Include visual acuity and funduscopic examination in surveillance of relevant late effects.

recognition: The late-effects table associates cranial radiation and Antimetabolites with neurocognitive late effects and clinical leukencephalopathy, and Brain surgery with neurocognitive deficits.

management.actions: Provide access to neuropsychological assessment and appropriate rehabilitation and support.

prevention: Perform neuropsychological evaluation and neurological examination during risk-adapted follow-up.
In children aged less than 12-36 months, radiotherapy may be delayed to reduce long-term sequelae, especially neurocognitive dysfunction.

recognition: The document identifies hearing impairment after platinum agents and lists ototoxicity among potential late effects of Heavy metals and cranial radiation.
prevention: Include audiological evaluation in risk-adapted follow-up.

toxicities.event: Reduced bone mineral density and osteonecrosis
recognition: The late-effects table links reduced bone mineral density to Antimetabolites and Corticosteroids, and osteonecrosis to Corticosteroids.
prevention: Use bone density evaluation for these exposures and musculoskeletal examination after Corticosteroids.

recognition: Peripheral sensory or motor neuropathy is listed as a potential late effect.
prevention: Include neurological examination in follow-up.

recognition: Children exposed to irradiation, including cranial radiotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, have increased risk of subsequent tumours such as malignant glioma or meningioma.
prevention: Include physical, neurological and skin examinations in surveillance; consider CNS imaging when clinical findings warrant it.

recognition: The late-effects table lists cerebrovascular complications after Cranial radiation and artery disease after Spine radiation.
prevention: Include neurological examination in follow-up.

recognition: Cardiac toxicity is listed among potential late effects of Spine radiation.
prevention: Include blood pressure assessment, cardiac examination, Echo and ECG in follow-up.

recognition: The late-effects table lists colorectal cancer as a potential effect of Spine radiation.
prevention: Provide colorectal cancer screening.

recognition: Scoliosis/ kyphosis is listed as a potential late effect of both exposures.
prevention: Examine the back and spine during follow-up.

recognition: Dental abnormalities are listed among potential late effects of this combined exposure.
prevention: Include dental examination and cleaning in follow-up.

toxicities.event: Psychosocial difficulties, mental health disorders, fatigue and sleep problems
recognition: The late-effects table lists adverse psychosocial or quality-of-life effects, mental health disorders, fatigue and sleep problems for children with a paediatric CNS tumour.
Mental health assessment may address depression, anxiety, post – traumatic stress and suicidal ideation.

management.actions: Provide access to psychosocial support, rehabilitation and guidance for school and family life.

prevention: Assess psychosocial health, educational or vocational progress and social withdrawal during follow-up; do not restrict visits to medical assessment alone.

recognition: The imaging section raises concern about long-term gadolinium deposition.
prevention: Use macrocyclic gadolinium-based contrast agents.

toxicities.event: Perioperative bleeding, fluid shifts and coagulopathy
recognition: These complications can develop rapidly, particularly during surgery for large, vascular tumours in small children.
prevention: Ensure specialist paediatric anaesthesia and access to paediatric intensive care.
For large vascular tumours, particularly choroid plexus tumours in small children, pre-operative embolization can reduce tumour vascularity and make resection safer.

recognition: Surgery involving the chiasm, optic radiations or occipital lobes may cause postoperative VF or VA deficits.
Posterior fossa ependymoma or medulloblastoma surgery may cause cranial nerve or gaze deficits, ocular misalignment and nystagmus.
Optic nerve dissection or abrupt interruption of its vascular supply after decompressive shunting may cause sudden, often irreversible VA or VF loss.
prevention: Aim to remove as much tumour as possible without increasing morbidity or mortality.
Use intra-operative neuro-monitoring where indicated to help preserve neurological function.

toxicities.event: Post-treatment imaging changes that can mimic tumour progression
toxicities.incidence: Temporary imaging effects termed pseudo-progression are described in up to 30-40% of cases receiving chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
recognition: Pseudo-progression may involve an enlarging contrast-enhancing lesion or increased FLAIR/T2 abnormality.
In this setting, pseudo response mainly refers to reduced enhancement after anti-angiogenic therapy.

management.severity: New enhancement or increased residual tumour size within the irradiated field during the first 12 weeks after irradiation
management.actions: Do not classify the finding as true progression unless histology or a follow-up scan after at least 4-6 weeks confirms it.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Provide age- and risk-adapted access to fertility preservation and consider sperm, oocyte or ovarian tissue cryopreservation, ideally before gonadotoxic treatment.
prophylaxis.target_population: Children and adolescents who may receive gonadotoxic therapy
prophylaxis.duration: Prior to start of gonadotoxic treatment

prophylaxis.recommendation: Screen survivors according to treatment-related risks so that late effects can be identified and addressed early.
prophylaxis.target_population: Children and adolescents treated for a CNS tumour

prophylaxis.recommendation: Use macrocyclic gadolinium-based contrast agents because of concern about long-term gadolinium deposition.
Radiotherapy may be delayed to minimise long-term sequelae, particularly neurocognitive dysfunction.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents diagnosed with a CNS tumour
decision_rules: Select treatment according to tumour type, location, stage, genetic characteristics, age and the relationship of the tumour to vital structures.
Some tumour types can be observed without immediate intervention, while others can be cured by surgery alone or require combined surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy.
Balance the expected benefit of each modality against acute and long-term toxicity, including neuropsychological effects.
Plan care through ongoing communication among the relevant specialties.

response_assessment.method: MRI of the whole head and spine for tumour staging
response_assessment.interpretation: Indicated for all tumour types, with a possible exception for craniopharyngioma.

response_assessment.timepoint: Early after surgery, within 72h post-OP; assessment is optimal within the first 48 hours
response_assessment.method: Contrast-enhanced MRI, compared with preoperative imaging and interpreted alongside the surgical report
response_assessment.interpretation: Determine the extent of resection; CT is not acceptable for this purpose. Postoperative changes and haemostatic materials can cause enhancement that resembles residual tumour.

response_assessment.method: Assess residual tumour using R0, R1, R2, R3 and R4
response_assessment.interpretation: R0: MRI shows no residual tumour and agrees with the neurosurgical report. R1: MRI shows no residuum, but the surgeon describes a small residuum or the surgical result is unknown. R2: MRI shows a residuum with maximum diameter < 5mm in any plane, or a thin residuum along or beyond the surgical margins. R3: measurable residuum ≥ 5mm in all 3 planes. R4: tumour size is unchanged or has changed only minimally from before surgery.

response_assessment.timepoint: Within 2-3 weeks after surgery if extensive postoperative changes impede assessment
response_assessment.interpretation: Further evaluate possible residual disease when surgical changes obscure it or resemble infiltration.

response_assessment.timepoint: During follow-up, according to the individual trial protocol
response_assessment.method: Compare tumour dimensions on comparable MRI sequences; use post-contrast T1 for uniformly enhancing tumours and consider T2/FLAIR, PD or pre-contrast T1 for heterogeneous, poorly enhancing or non-enhancing tumours
response_assessment.interpretation: If contrast behaviour changes, compare measurements made with the same sequence on the previous staging MRI. For multiple lesions, use the sum of the volumes of the 5 largest lesions.

response_assessment.method: Assess MRI tumour volume and new lesions using CR, PR, SD, MR and PD
response_assessment.interpretation: CR: no residual or recurrent tumour or meningeal dissemination. PR: tumour volume reduction ≥ 50% relative to the previous staging MRI; for meningeal disease, a considerable reduction. SD: tumour volume between ≤ 50% decrease in size and ≤ 25% increase in size, without significant change in meningeal dissemination. MR is used in some trials for a 50% to 25% decrease in tumour volume. PD: tumour volume increase ≥ 25% or a new lesion.

response_assessment.timepoint: When MRI findings are equivocal for progression or resolution
response_assessment.interpretation: Distinguish true change from pseudo progression or pseudo response. If progression is confirmed, assign its date to the first scan showing the abnormality.

supportive_care: Provide risk-adapted long-term screening for persistent and treatment-related effects.
Maintain access to rehabilitation, neuropsychological and psychosocial support.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The treating physician remains responsible for applying treatment to each child or adolescent. Approaches to progression or relapse are individual and are not covered by the guideline.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents for whom observation is appropriate on the basis of tumour type
decision_rules: Certain tumour types may be managed initially with observation alone; the overview does not identify which types qualify.

recommended_regimens.name: watch and wait
recommended_regimens.summary: Observation without immediate tumour-directed treatment is possible for some CNS tumour types.

response_assessment.method: MRI according to the applicable individual protocol
response_assessment.interpretation: Assess change using comparable scans and sequences.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: No tumour-specific eligibility criteria for observation are supplied.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents undergoing diagnostic or therapeutic neurosurgery
decision_rules: Use biopsy when tissue is needed to establish an integrated diagnosis or identify possible therapeutic targets.
Remove tumour tissue or accumulated CSF to relieve intracranial or spinal cord pressure when a complete resection is not feasible.
Aim to remove as much tumour as safely possible without increasing morbidity or mortality; pursue gross-total resection when appropriate.
Consider the greater prognostic importance of resection extent where fewer postoperative options exist; more radio- or chemosensitive tumours may be curable despite limited resection.
For selected infants with large tumours in critical locations, limited initial surgery followed by neoadjuvant chemotherapy and a second-look procedure has been beneficial.

recommended_regimens.name: Surgery
recommended_regimens.summary: Neurosurgical goals include obtaining diagnostic tissue, relieving pressure and resecting tumour to the safest feasible extent.

response_assessment.timepoint: Within 72h post-OP, preferably within the first 48 hours
response_assessment.method: Contrast-enhanced MRI and review of the neurosurgical report
response_assessment.interpretation: Establish the extent of resection and assess possible residual tumour.

supportive_care: Ensure access to specialist paediatric anaesthesia and paediatric intensive care.
Arrange rehabilitation and neuropsychological support when needed.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The surgical plan should be developed within the multidisciplinary team. Histopathological, genetic and biological tumour characterisation should be obtained before postoperative adjuvant therapy.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children presenting with raised intracranial pressure associated with a CNS tumour
decision_rules: Obtain urgent head imaging when raised intracranial pressure is suspected.
Choose an approach according to the cause of impaired CSF circulation and whether the tumour is operable.

recommended_regimens.name: tumour resection
recommended_regimens.summary: Resection can restore CSF circulation when the causative tumour is operable.

alternative_regimens.name: CSF drainage
alternative_regimens.summary: An internal or external drain can be used to re-establish CSF flow.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Select according to the underlying cause and tumour operability.

alternative_regimens.name: endoscopic 3rd ventriculostomy
alternative_regimens.summary: An endoscopic procedure can restore CSF circulation.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Select according to the underlying cause and tumour operability.

alternative_regimens.summary: May be used in addition to a surgical approach to treat raised intracranial pressure.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Adjunctive management of raised intracranial pressure.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Infratentorial tumours obstructing the fourth ventricle are described as the most common tumour-related cause in children.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with spinal cord compression or cauda equina syndrome caused by a new intraspinal mass
decision_rules: Contact neurosurgery directly for a new intraspinal mass.
Assess whether surgical reduction of the mass is feasible; if it is not, initiate radiotherapy as soon as possible.

recommended_regimens.name: debulking surgery
recommended_regimens.summary: Surgical reduction is considered when the compressive mass can be operated on.

alternative_regimens.name: radiotherapy
alternative_regimens.summary: An option that should begin as soon as possible when surgical debulking cannot be performed.

alternative_regimens.name: High-dose steroids
alternative_regimens.summary: Can lessen symptoms by reducing swelling.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Symptomatic spinal cord compression or cauda equina syndrome.

supportive_care: Treat urinary retention or incontinence and constipation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Neurological recovery can take time even after prompt mass removal. Compression may first appear at diagnosis or develop during treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents whose tumour requires radiotherapy
decision_rules: Determine radiation dose, fractionation, target volumes and technique according to tumour type and size, radiosensitivity, CNS maturation and the tolerance of adjacent structures.
In children aged less than 12-36 months, radiotherapy may be deferred to reduce the risk of long-term sequelae, particularly neurocognitive dysfunction.
Discuss the option of PBT for every child within the multidisciplinary team, while recognising that conclusive evidence from large prospective studies is scarce.
For treatment with curative intent, use highly conformal radiotherapy.

recommended_regimens.name: radiotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: An integral treatment modality for CNS tumour entities in which irradiation cannot be omitted.

alternative_regimens.name: PBT
alternative_regimens.summary: Its potential to reduce side effects, especially late effects, warrants individual multidisciplinary discussion.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider for each child; refer selected patients for proton beam or particle beam therapy in accordance with national clinical guidelines.

not_recommended.name: radiotherapy delivered by a clinical/radiation oncologist without a special interest or experience in paediatric radiotherapy
not_recommended.reason: The guidance advises against this for both curative and palliative treatment.

response_assessment.timepoint: During the first 12 weeks after irradiation ends
response_assessment.method: Review MRI enhancement or residual tumour growth in the irradiated field; if necessary, obtain histological confirmation or a short-interval scan after at least 4-6 weeks
response_assessment.interpretation: Do not classify new enhancement or growth within this interval and field as true progression unless confirmed. If follow-up MRI confirms growth, date progression from the first scan that documented it.

supportive_care: Review patients regularly during radiotherapy to address adverse effects and provide support.
Provide access to follow-up clinics for late effects.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Prospective collection of efficacy and toxicity outcomes after PBT is encouraged. Irradiation planning must also consider the lens, optic nerve, optic chiasma, brain stem and cervical medulla.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with progressive disease after surgery or for whom surgery is not feasible
decision_rules: Radiotherapy is indicated when disease progresses after surgery or surgery cannot be performed.

recommended_regimens.name: radiotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Indicated for progressive disease following surgery or when surgery is infeasible.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The overview does not provide a tumour-specific radiation dose or schedule.

decision_rules: Include radiotherapy in treatment for all children in this group.

recommended_regimens.name: radiotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Indicated for children with high grade glioma.

decision_rules: Consider craniospinal radiotherapy for all patients meeting the stated age criterion.

recommended_regimens.name: craniospinal radiotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Should be considered for patients aged more 3-5 years.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The age criterion is expressed as more 3-5 years; the overview does not resolve it to a single threshold.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients aged >12 months after surgical resection
decision_rules: Consider radiotherapy after resection for all patients above the stated age threshold.

recommended_regimens.name: radiotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Should be considered following surgical resection in patients aged >12 months.

response_assessment.method: MRI assessment and precise measurement of residual tumour
response_assessment.interpretation: Residual disease informs decisions about adjuvant treatment and possible second-look surgery.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Multidisciplinary national panels in the SIOP Ependymoma II trial evaluate residual disease for possible second-look surgery; the document says there is no clear or published evidence that centralised review is consistently beneficial.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with germ cell tumours other than completely resected pure mature teratomas
decision_rules: Include radiotherapy within multimodality treatment unless the tumour is a completely resected pure mature teratoma.

recommended_regimens.name: radiotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Required as part of multimodality treatment for the stated population.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Completely resected pure mature teratomas are expressly excluded from this radiotherapy indication.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients after surgery
decision_rules: Consider postoperative radiotherapy on an individual risk basis.

recommended_regimens.name: radiotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: A postoperative option for individual consideration according to risk.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: MRI staging of the whole head and spine has a possible exception for craniopharyngioma; CT may additionally be needed to show calcification when this diagnosis is suspected.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with ATRT for whom radiotherapy is planned
decision_rules: Generally follow the radiotherapy principles used for medulloblastoma.

recommended_regimens.name: radiotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Radiotherapy principles generally follow those for medulloblastoma.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: No ATRT-specific radiation regimen or age threshold is given.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with rare embryonal tumours for whom radiotherapy is planned
decision_rules: For rare embryonal tumours, generally use the radiotherapy principles applied to medulloblastoma.

recommended_regimens.name: radiotherapy
recommended_regimens.summary: The radiotherapy approach for rare embryonal tumours generally follows medulloblastoma principles.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: This statement concerns rare embryonal tumours; no corresponding radiation approach is specified for sarcomatous tumours.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with choroid plexus tumours
decision_rules: Determine whether to use radiotherapy according to the tumour subtype and extent of resection.
Where appropriate, consider preoperative embolization to reduce tumour vascularity and facilitate safer, more complete resection, particularly in a small child.

alternative_regimens.name: radiotherapy
alternative_regimens.summary: Use depends on the specific subtype and how extensively the tumour has been resected.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Individual subtype and extent of resection.

alternative_regimens.name: Pre-operative embolization
alternative_regimens.summary: Can reduce vascularity and alter tumour consistency to facilitate resection.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Particularly relevant for a large vascular tumour in a small child.

response_assessment.interpretation: Complete resection is associated with a better prognosis for both papillomas and carcinomas.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: No subtype-specific radiotherapy criteria are supplied.

decision_rules: The overview identifies mTOR inhibitors as targeted agents used in treatment but provides no eligibility rule or regimen.

alternative_regimens.summary: Identified as a targeted treatment used for SEGA.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: No individual drug, dose or treatment duration is specified.

decision_rules: The overview identifies BRAF and MEK inhibitors as targeted treatments used in low grade glioma without specifying selection criteria.
Molecular findings can guide tailored treatment; obtaining tumour tissue has consequently become relevant even for some optic pathway gliomas previously managed on a radiological diagnosis.

alternative_regimens.name: BRAF inhibitors
alternative_regimens.summary: Named among targeted treatments used for low grade glioma.

alternative_regimens.name: MEK inhibitors
alternative_regimens.summary: Named among targeted treatments used for low grade glioma.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: No specific molecular eligibility criterion, individual drug, dose or duration is provided.

decision_rules: Intrathecal or intraventricular treatment may be indicated when tumour spreads through the leptomeninges.

alternative_regimens.name: intrathecal therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: A possible route of treatment for leptomeningeal spread.

alternative_regimens.name: intraventricular therapy
alternative_regimens.summary: A possible route of treatment, including administration via an Ommaya reservoir.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document does not name a drug or specify which patients should receive either route.

decision_rules: This approach is standard in some protocols and is under investigation in ongoing clinical trials; the overview does not establish it as a general treatment for all CNS tumours.

alternative_regimens.summary: Used as standard treatment in some protocols and studied in ongoing trials; improved tumour exposure to cytotoxic drugs is described as theoretical.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: No tumour entity, agent combination, dose or schedule is specified.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with a pineal tumour and negative tumour markers
decision_rules: Obtain a biopsy to establish whether resection is required.
If pathology identifies a germinoma, do not perform further surgery; if it identifies an astrocytoma or embryonal tumour, proceed to formal resection.
When obstructive hydrocephalus is present, it can be treated during the same endoscopic procedure.

recommended_regimens.name: endoscopic biopsy
recommended_regimens.summary: Provides a tissue diagnosis that determines the need for further surgery.

response_assessment.interpretation: A germinoma requires no further surgery; an astrocytoma or embryonal tumour requires formal resection.

supportive_care: If obstructive hydrocephalus accompanies the pineal tumour, consider endoscopic third ventriculostomy during the biopsy procedure.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Brain tumour survivors with established GH deficiency
decision_rules: GH can be administered when GH deficiency has been established.
Recent guidelines advise waiting until the patient has been disease free for at least one year, while acknowledging that this timing rests on little evidence.

For a patient who may never become disease free, such as one with low grade glioma, discuss potential benefits and harms individually with the paediatric endocrinologist, oncologist, patient and parents.

recommended_regimens.name: GH
recommended_regimens.summary: Replacement treatment may be given to survivors with confirmed GH deficiency, subject to individual consideration of disease status.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Several large cohort studies found no increased risk of original-tumour recurrence or secondary tumours among survivors treated with GH compared with survivors not treated with GH; the document states that prospective confirmation is needed.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The optimal time to start treatment after complete remission and the optimal GH dose remain uncertain.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children with central diabetes insipidus after a localised CNS tumour or surgery
decision_rules: Involve an experienced paediatric endocrinologist in treatment.
When thirst regulation is impaired or ACTH deficiency coexists, monitor plasma sodium and fluid intake regularly.

recommended_regimens.name: oral desmopressin
recommended_regimens.summary: Generally manages central diabetes insipidus effectively.

response_assessment.method: Monitor plasma sodium and fluid intake
response_assessment.interpretation: Particularly relevant when thirst regulation is altered or ACTH deficiency is concurrent.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document attributes central diabetes insipidus to tumour- or surgery-related damage of the hypothalamus, pituitary stalk or pituitary gland, and states that it does not occur as a late effect of radiotherapy.

special_populations.considerations: Long-term effects of radiotherapy, particularly neurocognitive dysfunction, are a concern in this age group.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Radiotherapy may be delayed to reduce the risk of long-term sequelae.

special_populations.population: Infants with large tumours in critical locations
special_populations.considerations: The tumour location may limit the extent of safe initial surgery.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: In specific cases, limited initial surgery followed by a second-look procedure after neoadjuvant chemotherapy has been beneficial.

special_populations.population: Children with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) and optic pathway gliomas (OPG)
special_populations.considerations: Approximately 15% of children with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) have OPG. Its course is indolent in up to 70 - 85%, whereas about 15% - 30% develop more aggressive disease with visual deficits.

special_populations.population: Children with sellar or suprasellar tumours or hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction at diagnosis
special_populations.considerations: Hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction may already be present at diagnosis. These children should be referred directly to a paediatric endocrinologist for individual monitoring and, when needed, treatment of endocrine deficiencies.

special_populations.population: Children treated with cranial or cranio-spinal radiotherapy
special_populations.considerations: Hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction may emerge after treatment and become more prevalent over time. Cranio-spinal radiotherapy also exposes children to risks involving the thyroid and spinal growth. Risk-adapted endocrine surveillance is indicated; children who received cranio-spinal irradiation should have yearly TSH and FT4 testing and neck palpation.

special_populations.population: Children with central diabetes insipidus (CDI) and impaired thirst regulation or concurrent ACTH deficiency
special_populations.considerations: Management may be difficult, particularly after hypothalamic damage associated with low grade glioma or craniopharyngioma. Regular assessment of plasma sodium and fluid intake is necessary.

special_populations.population: Female survivors exposed to alkylating agents or radiotherapy involving the ovaries or hypothalamic pituitary region
special_populations.considerations: These exposures increase the risk of premature ovarian insufficiency. The document recommends monitoring growth and pubertal development, with yearly LH/FSH/estradiol assessment. Fertility preservation should be considered, ideally before gonadotoxic treatment.

special_populations.population: Male survivors exposed to alkylating agents or radiotherapy involving the hypothalamic pituitary region or potential old spinal fields
special_populations.considerations: Counselling about gonadotoxicity is recommended. At-risk pre-pubertal and peripubertal survivors should have growth and pubertal progression monitored; for postpubertal survivors, early-morning total serum testosterone testing at clinically appropriate intervals is reasonable. Fertility preservation should be considered, ideally before gonadotoxic treatment.

special_populations.population: Brain tumour survivors with established GH deficiency
special_populations.considerations: Most current recommendations advise that GH can be given safely after GH deficiency is established. Recent guidelines recommend waiting until the patient has been disease free for at least one year, although the document notes that evidence for this interval is limited. Some children with low grade glioma may never be disease free; in those cases, the potential benefits and harms require individual discussion among the paediatric endocrinologist, oncologist, patient and parents.

special_populations.population: Children with newly diagnosed CNS tumours and visual signs
special_populations.considerations: The document calls for multidisciplinary evaluation and management of visual impairment, together with referral to a dedicated visual rehabilitation service. Infants and young children are particularly vulnerable to underreporting of visual symptoms and to additional visual loss during visual development.

conditions.name: CNS tumours
synonyms: tumours of the central nervous system
conditions.description: This heterogeneous group includes tumours whose course and long-term outcome vary with histology, age at diagnosis, location, disease stage and tumour genetics. Diagnosis integrates tissue morphology with immunohistochemical, genetic and epigenetic findings.
conditions.epidemiology: In high-income countries, these tumours account for one quarter of neoplasms in children and adolescents up to the age of 18 years and are the most common solid tumours in this population. Reported incidence differs among European countries; registry practices, diagnostic access and genuine variation may contribute.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptoms depend on age, tumour site and aggressiveness. Up to one half of patients have raised intracranial pressure, often from impaired CSF circulation with a posterior fossa tumour. Possible manifestations include headache, vomiting, behavioural or concentration changes, reduced appetite, weight loss, fatigue, lethargy and increased sleep. Young children may develop an enlarging head circumference. Site-dependent manifestations include focal neurological, visual, endocrine and spinal symptoms.

Determine the extent of resection and assess residual tumour.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A persisting abnormal signal and/or enhancement resembling the pre-operative tumour may represent residual disease. Assessment should also consider the operative report and changes caused by surgery.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide imaging when surgery is too urgent to await MRI, or show calcification in selected cases.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Exceptionally before very urgent surgery, or additionally when calcification needs assessment, such as suspected craniopharyngioma.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: CT is not acceptable for determining the extent of resection after surgery.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Morphology alone may not distinguish tumours with similar histology but substantially different biology and clinical behaviour.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Classify tumour differentiation and assess copy-number alterations.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: If required tests were incomplete, the most precise supported diagnosis is supplemented with NOS; if comprehensive testing does not match an established WHO tumour type, NEC is added.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess molecular alterations relevant to integrated diagnosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A single alteration may not establish tumour type because alterations can occur across tumour types or coexist.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect gene fusions.
Assess somatic mutations and pathogenic inherited variants.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Desirable using the same testing approach.

definitions.description: Post-operative MRI shows no residual tumour, consistent with the neurosurgical report.
MRI shows no residual tumour, but the surgeon describes a small remnant or the surgical result is unknown.
MRI shows a small remnant with maximum diameter < 5mm in any plane, or a thin remnant along or beyond the surgical margins.
The remnant is measurable and ≥ 5mm in all 3 planes.
Tumour size is unchanged or has changed only minimally from the pre-operative state, for example following biopsy.

staging.additional_rules: These categories apply only to early postoperative MRI and should be assigned in conjunction with the neurosurgical report. Use “unclear” if imaging is inadequate or the operative cavity cannot be interpreted reliably.

prognostic_tools.name: CR, PR, SD, MR and PD response criteria

risk_groups.criteria: No residual or recurrent tumour and no meningeal dissemination.
Tumour volume falls by ≥ 50% relative to the previous staging MRI; for meningeal disease, a considerable reduction is used.
Tumour volume lies between ≤ 50% decrease in size and ≤ 25% increase in size relative to the previous staging MRI, without significant change in meningeal dissemination.
A 50% to 25% decrease in tumour volume; this category is used in some trials.
Tumour volume increases by ≥ 25%, or a new lesion appears.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: These are neuroradiological response categories rather than survival-risk groups. During the first 12 weeks after irradiation, new or increased enhancement within the irradiated field should not be classified as true progression without histological confirmation or a follow-up scan after at least 4-6 weeks.

follow_up.schedule: Follow-up MRI timing follows the individual trial protocol. Long-term surveillance should be adapted to treatment-related risk.
recommended_tests: Follow-up MRI using comparable sequences to measure tumour size and assess response
long_term_effects: Neurocognitive, behavioural, emotional and adaptive difficulties
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Late effects may persist from diagnosis or arise after treatment. Their early recognition and management aim to improve quality of survival.

conditions.name: Low grade glioma (LGG)
conditions.description: The guideline covers low-grade glioma as a distinct CNS tumour group; its course can include indolent disease or progression, depending on the lesion.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Symptoms of slow-growing low-grade tumours can be misdiagnosed for long periods, with diagnosis delayed up to several years. Manifestations vary with tumour location.

subtypes.name: optic pathway gliomas (OPG)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: These lesions primarily affect vision and range from stable disease to repeated progression.

subtypes.distinguishing_features: Listed as a new entity in WHO classification 2021.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Diagnose and stage CNS disease.

recommended_tests: Assessment for endocrine and visual dysfunction when relevant
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The document identifies unresolved questions about when to start GH treatment in children who have GHD and persistent low-grade glioma.

conditions.name: optic pathway gliomas (OPG)
conditions.description: These predominantly low-grade gliomas infiltrate the visual pathways. Their clinical course ranges from stable, indolent disease to repeated progression.
conditions.epidemiology: Approximately 15% of children with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) have OPG. Among NF1-associated OPG, up to 70 - 85% have an indolent course, while about 15% - 30% behave more aggressively and cause visual deficits.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Visual impairment is frequently the principal or only presenting feature. Visual acuity and field defects may coexist; homonymous and bitemporal hemianopia are common field patterns. Of children with OPG, 5 - 10% meet criteria for legal blindness. Infants below 1 year of age and children with post-chiasmatic lesions appear more likely to lose visual acuity. Isolated optic nerve lesions may cause proptosis or optic pallor or atrophy; large hypothalamic-chiasmatic lesions may produce hydrocephalus, raised intracranial pressure and papilledema.

subtypes.name: isolated optic nerve gliomas (IONG)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: With or without NF1, these may cause proptosis and optic pallor or atrophy.

diagnostic_workup.test: MRI of the whole head and spine
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the tumour and stage CNS disease.
Document vision and identify deficits before treatment.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise visual function, optic disc findings and ocular alignment or movements.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During baseline visual assessment and subsequent evaluation as clinically appropriate.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Visual acuity should account for refractive error; visual field testing should use an age-appropriate method.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Provide an additional measure of retinal nerve fibre or ganglion cell layers.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cut-off of 76 µm has been used for abnormal OCT, and a change of ≥10% in specified layer thicknesses has been used for significant change over time. There is no clear consensus linking OCT change to progression or treatment response, so findings should be considered alongside functional measures.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Obtain molecular information for tailored treatment decisions.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The document notes an increased requirement for biopsy in optic pathway gliomas previously treated on a radiological diagnosis.

follow_up.schedule: Regular ophthalmological surveillance is suggested; frequency and duration depend on tumour location, treatment and the severity or risk of visual dysfunction.
recommended_tests: Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT) in selected cases
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Functional visual findings should accompany interpretation of OCT changes.

recommendations.statement: Obtain additional CT in selected cases, such as suspected craniopharyngioma, when calcification needs to be demonstrated.

recommendations.statement: Acquire all imaging studies in accordance with the SIOPE-BTG neuroimaging protocol.
recommendations.rationale: Standardized acquisition supports comparisons across time points and centres.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 5. Summary

recommendations.statement: Make preoperative contrast-enhanced MRI available for every patient.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 5. Summary

recommendations.statement: Acquire preoperative 3D images for surgical and RT planning.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 5. Summary

recommendations.statement: Make an early postoperative contrast-enhanced MRI available for every patient within 72h post-OP, including ventilated patients.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 5. Summary

recommendations.statement: Have designated specialists experienced in paediatric neuroimaging report scans according to protocol guidance.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 5. Summary

recommendations.statement: Obtain baseline spine MRI before resection or biopsy, or 10-14 days afterward.
recommendations.rationale: Postoperative blood products and dural enhancement can interfere with interpretation.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 5. Summary

recommendations.statement: Use the same Tesla-strength at successive study examinations.
recommendations.rationale: Consistency improves comparison between scans.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 5. Summary

recommendations.statement: Use comparable sequences on successive study scans.
recommendations.rationale: Comparable acquisition supports assessment over time.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 5. Summary

recommendations.statement: Repeat MRI within 2-3 weeks after surgery if postoperative changes obscure residual disease assessment or resemble tumour infiltration.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 5. Summary

recommendations.statement: Do not use CT for routine brain imaging in children with a cancer tumour.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 5. Summary

recommendations.statement: Have designated radiologists or neuroradiologists available for every child with a brain tumour.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 3. Essential quality parameters

recommendations.statement: Use macrocyclic gadolinium-based contrast agents.
recommendations.rationale: The document notes growing concern about long-term gadolinium deposition.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 6.1 MRI protocol Brain imaging

recommendations.statement: For tumours enhancing uniformly, measure diameters on post-contrast T1; for heterogeneous, poorly enhancing or non-enhancing tumours, consider T2/FLAIR or PD and pre-contrast T1.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 6.4 Follow-up MRI

recommendations.statement: When MRI findings cannot distinguish progression or resolution from pseudo-progression or pseudo-response, obtain an early follow-up scan if needed; once true progression is confirmed, assign its date to the first scan showing the abnormality.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 6.4 Follow-up MRI

recommendations.statement: Do not classify new enhancement or increased residual tumour size within the irradiated field during the first 12 weeks after irradiation as true progression unless histology or a follow-up scan after at least 4-6 weeks confirms it.
recommendations.rationale: Temporary treatment-related imaging changes may resemble progression.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 6.6.2 Response criteria

recommendations.statement: Use Dynamic Susceptibility Contrast (DSC) – MRI as the currently recommended contrast-injection perfusion method.
recommendations.context: Advanced MRI recommendations are not mandatory.
recommendations.rationale: Contrast-injection perfusion imaging remains less established in children, and aspects of its protocol are still being developed.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 6.7 Multi-Modal Advanced MRI

recommendations.statement: For DSC-MRI, give a pre-bolus of 0.05mmol/Kg Gd at least 2 minutes before a main injection of 0.05mmol/Kg Gd, yielding 0.1mmol/Kg Gd in total; standardize the injection rate at 3ml/sec.
recommendations.rationale: The pre-bolus is intended to reduce T1 effects; the protocol remains subject to development, particularly for very small infants.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 6.7 Multi-Modal Advanced MRI — Contrast Injection

recommendations.statement: Recommend four hours of fasting before PET tracer injection and use a head holder to limit motion artefacts.
recommendations.rationale: Fasting helps maintain stable metabolic conditions.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 6.8 PET Imaging

recommendations.statement: Apply iterative PET reconstruction or, alternatively, filtered back projection; apply attenuation, scatter, randoms, dead-time and decay corrections.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 6.8 PET Imaging

recommendations.statement: Do not use point-spread-function reconstruction for PET.
recommendations.rationale: This approach can produce artefacts.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 6.8 PET Imaging

recommendations.statement: Use PET voxel size < 3mm in every direction and spatial resolution < 6 mm FWHM.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 6.8 PET Imaging

recommendations.statement: Co-register PET with a recent MRI, ideally < 2 weeks old, preferentially T1W with contrast or FLAIR.
recommendations.rationale: Automatic co-registration may introduce errors in children.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 6.8 PET Imaging

recommendations.statement: Have diagnostic imaging specialists jointly integrate MRI and PET findings; report maximal tumour-to-background ratio (TBRmax) and metabolically active volume, and also maximal tumour-to-normal-striatum ratio (TSRmax) for DOPA PET.
recommendations.source_heading: IMAGING WORKING GROUP — 6.8 PET Imaging

recommendations.statement: Discuss each case regularly within the multidisciplinary team at presentation, diagnosis, after surgery, during adjuvant treatment and at recurrence; develop the neurosurgical plan within that team.

recommendations.statement: Include spinal surgical expertise when managing spinal tumours, particularly if deformity of the growing spine is present or anticipated.

recommendations.statement: Avoid oxidized methylcellulose (Surgicel) during paediatric brain tumour surgery.

recommendations.statement: Collect multiple specimens from different tumour regions and, during open procedures, obtain at least 1 x 1.5 cm3 or 3 x 0.5cm3 specimens.

recommendations.statement: Consider delaying radiotherapy in children aged less than 12-36 months.

recommendations.statement: For children exposed to cranial radiotherapy who are at risk of overweight or obesity, check BMI yearly, advise on diet and physical activity, and obtain endocrine consultation when BMI > + 2 SD.
recommendations.context: Risk factors listed are age < 4 years and radiation dose > 20 Gy.
recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Hypothalamic-pituitary function screening

recommendations.statement: Monitor Tanner stage together with growth velocity every 6 months when screening for precocious puberty after cranial radiotherapy.
recommendations.context: The table defines precocious puberty as B2 <8 yr ♀ or testes 4+ cc <9 yr ♂; listed risk factors are young age and radiation dose to the pituitary region > 18 Gy.
recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Hypothalamic-pituitary function screening

recommendations.statement: Assess symptoms of TSH deficiency and measure TSH and FT4 yearly when screening for central hypothyroidism after cranial radiotherapy.
recommendations.context: Listed risk factors are young age and radiation dose to the pituitary region > 40 Gy.
recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Hypothalamic-pituitary function screening

recommendations.statement: After GH treatment starts, refer to an endocrinologist if FT4 is below its reference interval on 2 separate occasions or declines by > 20 % over time.
recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Hypothalamic-pituitary function screening

recommendations.statement: Assess Tanner stage and growth velocity every 6 months when screening for LH/FSH deficiency after cranial radiotherapy.
recommendations.context: The table lists radiation dose to the pituitary region > 40 Gy as a risk factor and describes the finding as B2 > 12 yr ♀ or testes 4+ cc > 13 yr ♂.
recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Hypothalamic-pituitary function screening

recommendations.statement: Ask about adrenal insufficiency and measure 08:00 AM morning cortisol yearly; refer directly to an endocrinologist if ACTHD is suspected.
recommendations.context: Screening after cranial radiotherapy; listed risk factors are young age and radiation dose to the pituitary region > 40 Gy.
recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Hypothalamic-pituitary function screening

recommendations.statement: Record height, weight, sitting height and BMI every 6 months and refer to an endocrinologist if the growth trajectory declines.
recommendations.context: Screening for GH deficiency after cranial radiotherapy; listed risk factors are young age and radiation dose > 18 Gy.
recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Hypothalamic-pituitary function screening

recommendations.statement: After neck irradiation, measure TSH and FT4 and palpate the neck yearly; refer for endocrine assessment when FT4 is low, TSH is high or a thyroid nodule is palpable.
recommendations.context: Thyroid surveillance, including after craniospinal irradiation.
recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Thyroid function screening

recommendations.statement: Consider thyroid ultrasound to monitor for nodules or thyroid cancer.
recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Thyroid function screening

recommendations.statement: Discuss the surveillance method and frequency for thyroid cancer with the patient and parents according to individual needs.
recommendations.context: The document attributes this recommendation to IGHG guidance for survivors at risk.
recommendations.rationale: The document describes potential benefits of early detection alongside uncertain treatment benefit, false results, anxiety, unnecessary procedures and possible overtreatment.
recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Thyroid function screening

recommendations.statement: Monitor growth, pubertal development and LH/FSH/estradiol yearly in female survivors exposed to alkylating agents or radiotherapy involving the ovaries or hypothalamic-pituitary region.
recommendations.rationale: The document identifies these exposures as increasing the risk of POI.
recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Gonadal function screening

recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Gonadal function screening

recommendations.statement: For at-risk pre-pubertal and peripubertal male survivors, monitor growth and pubertal development and progression, including Tanner stage, to screen for testosterone deficiency.
recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Gonadal function screening

recommendations.statement: In postpubertal males, consider early-morning total serum testosterone testing at clinically appropriate intervals to monitor for testosterone deficiency.
recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Gonadal function screening

recommendations.statement: Consider fertility preservation, including sperm, oocyte or ovarian tissue cryopreservation, ideally before gonadotoxic treatment.
recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Gonadal function screening

recommendations.statement: Refer children with falling growth velocity, stalled pubertal progression, abnormal laboratory results or a history suggestive of pituitary deficiency to a paediatric endocrinologist.
recommendations.source_heading: ENDOCRINE SURVEILLANCE IN CHILDREN WITH BRAIN CNS TUMORS — Indications for referral

recommendations.statement: GH may be administered to brain tumour survivors with established GH deficiency; recent guidelines recommend waiting until the patient has been disease free for at least one year.

recommendations.statement: Arrange a baseline neuro-ophthalmological assessment for every child newly diagnosed with a CNS neoplasm, irrespective of tumour location.
recommendations.context: The assessment includes refraction, VA, VF, fundoscopy and orthoptic assessment under RAFFO.
