document_sections.heading: OVERVIEW AND DISCIPLINE GROUPS
document_sections.content: This guideline addresses treatment of CNS tumours in children and adolescents in Europe. The treating physician retains responsibility for applying procedures and treatments to individual patients.

document_sections.heading: 1. Introduction
document_sections.content: CNS tumours are the most common solid neoplasms in children and adolescents. Their histological diversity, age at diagnosis, location, stage and genetic features contribute to markedly different courses and long-term outcomes. Management ranges from observation or surgery alone to combined surgery, chemotherapy, sometimes at high dose, and radiotherapy. More detailed MRI has improved tumour characterization and surgical planning. Neurosurgical advances include neuro-navigation, stereotactic techniques, intra-operative ultrasound and MRI, alongside better peri-operative support. Diagnosis of sampled tissue now integrates morphology with immunohistochemical, genetic and epigenetic findings; this has refined tumour subdivisions in the WHO classification of tumours of the central nervous system. Radiotherapy developments seek to lower doses, restrict fields or avoid irradiation when possible; adopted techniques include IMRT, Tomotherapy and Proton Beam Therapy. Care requires early and continuing coordination among paediatric (neuro)oncology, neurosurgery, neuroradiology, radiotherapy, neuropathology, neuropaediatrics, neuro-ophthalmology, endocrinology, rehabilitation and other disciplines. Increasing survival has made late effects important both when choosing initial therapy and during long-term follow-up. Separate chapters address disciplines and specific CNS tumour entities.

document_sections.heading: 2. Epidemiology
document_sections.content: In high-income countries, CNS tumours account for one quarter of neoplasms diagnosed up to the age of 18 years and form the largest group of solid childhood tumours. Reported incidence varies across Europe. Differences may reflect data sources, diagnostic access, true variation or differences in whether cancer registries exist and how completely they record cases. Limited diagnostic access may also cause underdiagnosis and variation in outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 3. Classification of tumours of the central nervous system
document_sections.content: Accurate histopathological and molecular identification of tumour type and grade is essential for treatment decisions, protocol selection and clinical-trial inclusion. Biopsy or resection specimens undergo standardized histological, immunohistochemical and molecular-pathological assessment under the current WHO classification of CNS tumours. Earlier WHO categories relied mainly on light microscopy and a malignancy scale estimating biological behaviour and natural course. Regular revisions increasingly incorporate molecularly defined entities. The 2021 version substantially changed diagnostic methods, nomenclature and grading, and introduced types or subtypes identifiable through technologies such as DNA methylation profiling. The entity-specific sections cover Low grade glioma (LGG), High-grade glioma (HGG), Ependymoma, Choroid plexus tumours, Medulloblastoma, Atypical teratoid rhabdoid tumours (ATRT), CNS Germ cell tumours, Craniopharyngioma, and Rare CNS embryonal and sarcomatous tumours.

document_sections.heading: 4. Aetiology and risk factors
document_sections.content: Most paediatric CNS tumours arise sporadically through random mutations or epigenetic changes. Irradiation and inherited predisposition are exceptions. Children exposed to irradiation, including cranial radiotherapy for acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, have increased risk of subsequent tumours such as malignant glioma or meningioma. Table 1 gives a non-exhaustive account of predisposition syndromes, their mutations and associated CNS tumours.

document_sections.heading: 5. Clinical presentation
document_sections.content: Symptoms depend on tumour site, patient age and tumour aggressiveness. High-grade tumours generally cause symptoms over days to weeks; slow-growing low-grade tumours may be misdiagnosed, delaying diagnosis for up to several years. Up to one half of patients present with raised intracranial pressure from obstructed CSF flow, most often with posterior fossa tumours. Manifestations include headache, vomiting that is commonly but not invariably early-morning, behavioural or concentration changes, poor appetite or refusal of food, weight loss potentially progressing to anorexia, rapid fatigue, lethargy and increased sleep. Head circumference may increase in young children before cranial sutures fuse. Compression or infiltration produces additional location-dependent neurological findings, illustrated non-exhaustively in Table 2. Age must also inform interpretation of symptoms. Figure 1 identifies symptom red flags by age group.

document_sections.heading: 6. Emergency situations Raised intracranial pressure
document_sections.content: Possible signs of raised intracranial pressure include vomiting, headache, bradycardia, hypoventilation, altered consciousness, irritability, seizures and focal deficits; papilloedema is possible but not required. Urgent head imaging is needed. In children, an infratentorial tumour compressing the fourth ventricle and obstructing CSF circulation is the most common cause. Management depends on cause and tumour operability. CSF circulation may be restored by tumour resection, internal or external drainage, or endoscopic 3rd ventriculostomy. Steroids and mannitol may supplement surgical measures.

document_sections.heading: Spinal cord compression and cauda equina syndrome
document_sections.content: SCC or CES may be the presenting manifestation of a spinal tumour or emerge during treatment from new metastasis or complications such as bleeding after lumbar puncture. Early features include back pain, urinary retention or incontinence, constipation and faecal incontinence; weakness, paralysis and sensory loss are later manifestations of SCC. A new intraspinal mass warrants immediate neurosurgical contact. High-dose steroids can improve symptoms by decreasing swelling. If debulking cannot be performed, radiotherapy is an option and should start as soon as possible. Neurological recovery can be delayed even after rapid removal. Management also requires effective analgesia, treatment of bladder and bowel symptoms, and early physiotherapy.

document_sections.heading: 7. Diagnostic modalities and staging – a short overview
document_sections.content: MRI is mandatory for diagnosing CNS tumours, apart from the very small number of patients needing exceptionally urgent surgery after CT. MRI depicts more anatomy than CT; diffusion, perfusion and MR spectroscopy can add diagnostic and planning information, including tractography. MR-linked neuro-navigation is standard operative care, and intraoperative MRI is increasingly used to support complete resection and avoid unnecessary repeat surgery. Postoperative resection extent must be assessed by MRI rather than CT. MRI of the whole head and spine is indicated for staging at diagnosis in every tumour type, with a possible exception for craniopharyngioma. Additional CT may be needed in selected cases, such as suspected craniopharyngioma, to identify calcification. SIOPE provides MRI guidance; tumour-specific sections describe staging approaches.

document_sections.heading: 8. Treatment modalities – a short overview
document_sections.content: Benefits of each modality must be weighed against acute and long-term toxicity, including neuropsychological deficits. Surgery contributes to management of all CNS tumour types, but its extent depends on location and proximity to vital structures. Its purposes are diagnostic biopsy and identification of therapeutic targets; removal of tumour or accumulated CSF to relieve intracranial or spinal pressure, avert a threat to life and improve quality of life even without complete resection; or gross-total resection. Although resection extent affects prognosis for many children, the usual aim is maximal removal without increasing morbidity or mortality. Extent matters more prognostically when postoperative options are limited, whereas radio- or chemosensitive tumours may be cured despite limited surgery. In specific cases, including infants with large tumours in critical sites, limited initial surgery followed by second-look surgery after neoadjuvant chemotherapy has been beneficial. Improved imaging and techniques have significantly increased operability. Chemotherapy agents and combinations vary by entity and usually consist of conventional agents. The bloodbrain-barrier ordinarily restricts cerebral drug concentrations, but altered transport and endothelial permeability at the tumour-blood barrier allow some systemic drugs to reach tumour tissue. Leptomeningeal spread may warrant intrathecal or intraventricular treatment, for example through an Ommaya reservoir. Myeloablative chemotherapy with stem cell recue might theoretically improve cytotoxic exposure; it is standard in some protocols and under investigation in ongoing trials. Examples of tumour-directed agents are mTOR inhibitors for SEGA and BRAF and MEK inhibitors for low grade glioma. Some tumour entities still require radiotherapy despite its toxicity and late effects. Tumour type and size, radiosensitivity and CNS maturity largely determine total dose, fractionation, target volumes and technique. Planning must also account for the tolerance of the lens, optic nerve, optic chiasma, brain stem and cervical medulla, as well as brain tissue. International standards seek accurate, reproducible, high-quality irradiation. Progression and relapse require individualized approaches and are outside this guideline.

document_sections.heading: 9. Follow-up care – a short overview
document_sections.content: As more children survive long term, substantial late effects have become more prominent. They can reflect persistent problems present since diagnosis, such as visual impairment, or new treatment-related conditions, such as endocrine effects after radiotherapy or hearing impairment after platinum agents. Early detection and treatment where possible may prevent or lessen harm; risk-adapted screening is therefore recommended. Long-term follow-up guidelines support such screening. Follow-up aims to improve quality of survival (QoS) and generate knowledge to refine initial treatment.

document_sections.heading: 1. Background
document_sections.content: Imaging of primary paediatric CNS tumours and possible CNS dissemination is central to care. Because these tumours are uncommon, multicentre research provides the strongest management evidence, making standardized acquisition essential across participating centres. Consistency enables comparison across pre-operative, postoperative and follow-up examinations and among centres. The European Society for Paediatric Oncology (SIOPE) Brain Tumour Imaging Working Group developed its protocol from group consensus and evidence from previous trials; it was ratified in December 2019 and is updated as practice and trial requirements evolve. Field-strength-specific protocols address 1.5 and 3 Tesla scanners. Hardware and software capabilities still vary considerably. Mandatory sequences represent the minimum needed for basic evaluation, while additional multimodal MRI is permitted. Guidance for MRS, DTI and perfusion imaging is not currently mandatory.

document_sections.heading: 2. Institutional requirements
document_sections.content: Institutions need 1.5 or 3T MRI scanners, trained radiology or neuroradiology specialists, and personnel able to provide sedation or anaesthesia for imaging when required.

document_sections.heading: 3. Essential quality parameters
document_sections.content: A designated radiologist or neuroradiologist with childhood brain-tumour expertise must be available for every patient.

document_sections.heading: 5. Summary
document_sections.content: The imaging summary distinguishes mandatory, desirable and discouraged practices. Imaging must follow the SIOPE-BTG neuroimaging protocol. Every patient must have contrast-enhanced pre-operative MRI and contrast-enhanced early postoperative MRI within 72h post-OP, including ventilated patients. Pre-operative 3D acquisition should support surgery and RT. Designated paediatric neuroimaging specialists must report examinations according to protocol. Baseline spinal MRI is recommended before biopsy or resection, or 10-14 days afterward, to limit interference from postoperative blood products and dural enhancement. Using the same Tesla-strength and comparable sequences at successive examinations is recommended. If postoperative changes obscure residual disease or resemble infiltration, repeat MRI within 2-3 weeks is recommended. CT should not be used for routine brain imaging in a child with a cancer tumour.

document_sections.heading: 6. Appendix: Imaging protocol for patients in European SIOP Brain Tumour Studies
document_sections.content: The appendix sets out brain and spinal imaging guidance, tumour measurement, postoperative and follow-up assessment, neuroradiological response definitions, advanced MRI and PET imaging.

document_sections.heading: 6.1 MRI protocol Brain imaging Essential sequences on 1.5T
document_sections.content: Essential brain-imaging protocols are specified for 1.5T and 3.0T. The named 3D gradient echo (GRE) acquisition is inversion recovery GRE (IR TFE/FFE). For 2D sequences, slice thickness is ≤ 4mm and interslice gap ≤ 1mm; a gap of 10 % of slice thickness is desirable. For very small lesions, consider thickness of 3mm or less. For 3D sequences, thickness is ≤ 1mm without a gap; isotropic resolution of 1mmx 1mm x 1mm is desirable when the scanner permits. Field of view is 230 mm, with a range of 220-250 mm according to head size. Minimum matrix size is 256; 512 is desirable for greater resolution and 96- 128 applies to EPI sequences. On 3.0T, T1 FLAIR, T1 inversion recovery (IR) or T1 gradient echo may replace a T1 SE sequence if diagnostic quality is preserved and the sequence remains consistent for that patient. Because of concern about long-term gadolinium deposition, macrocyclic gadolinium-based contrast agents are recommended. Optional 1.5T sequences may add information. A 3D FLAIR sequence can replace 2D FLAIR unless earlier examinations for the same patient used 2D imaging. Region-focused, heavily weighted T2w imaging helps assess poorly or non-enhancing extra-axial or parenchymal-surface lesions.

document_sections.heading: 6.2 Tumour measurement
document_sections.content: Where volumetric tools are unavailable, calculate tumour volume by the ellipsoid formula A x B x C x ½, using maximal antero-posterior, transverse and cranio-caudal dimensions. Additional 3D volumetric calculation is possible. Accurate measurements underpin follow-up evaluation and should be saved as annotated images where possible. For multiple lesions, obtain the sum of the 5 largest lesions; this approach requires further validation and may change. Individual trials may instead specify axial 2D measurements or other ways of measuring the 3 dimensions.

document_sections.heading: 6.3 Early postoperative imaging
document_sections.content: Assessment is optimal within the first 48 hours after surgery. Because nonspecific enhancement commonly appears after 3 days, postoperative MRI must occur within that interval. Haemostatic materials and electrocoagulation can nevertheless produce false-positive nodular enhancement earlier; interpret pre-contrast and post-contrast T1-weighted findings alongside T2-weighted and FLAIR signals. On the basis of a single-centre study and consensus, a final intraoperative MRI can serve as baseline only when acquired on a 3.0T scanner, following the SIOPE brain tumour protocol, under supervision of a radiologist experienced in paediatric brain tumours and reported jointly with the operating neurosurgeon. Pre-operative and final intraoperative sequences must be comparable. Resection after that scan disqualifies it as the final scan; another examination after the additional resection should use the complete SIOPE protocol. The national reference radiologist or radiology panel makes the final decision on accepting an intraoperative baseline. Comparison with pre-operative MRI is essential. Measure any residual lesion in all three planes; when it is clearest on T2-weighted images, include a second T2-weighted or FLAIR plane. Residual tumour means persistent abnormal signal and/or enhancement resembling the pre-operative tumour. DWI can reveal surgical or ischaemic injury that might alter enhancement and later interpretation. The surgical report is often useful and should be accessible.

document_sections.heading: 6.4 Follow-up MRI
document_sections.content: Schedule follow-up MRI according to the relevant trial protocol. Measure uniformly enhancing tumours on post-contrast T1 images. For heterogeneous, faintly enhancing or non-enhancing tumours, T2/FLAIR, PD or pre-contrast T1 may be informative. Treatment can diminish enhancement disproportionately to volume, so the best sequence may not be identifiable initially. In that situation, retain the original measurement sequence or, when changing sequences because enhancement changes, compare the same sequence across current and preceding staging scans. Equivocal apparent progression or resolution may require an earlier repeat examination to establish the true response. Once progression is confirmed, assign its time to the first scan showing the abnormality. In paediatric neuro-oncology, pseudo response principally describes reduced enhancement after anti-angiogenic treatment; assess response in that situation using T2 and FLAIR measurements.

document_sections.heading: 6.5 Definition of residual tumour
document_sections.content: These residual-disease categories apply only to early postoperative MRI and require interpretation alongside the neurosurgical report, because subtle residual tumour may be invisible on imaging. R0 means MRI shows no residual tumour and agrees with the operative report. R1 means MRI shows none, but the surgeon describes a small remainder or the operative result is unknown. R2 means MRI shows a small residual lesion with maximum diameter < 5mm in any plane, or a thin rim along or beyond the surgical margins. R3 means measurable residual tumour ≥ 5mm in all 3 planes. R4 means residual size is unchanged or only minimally different from before surgery, as may occur after biopsy. A thin enhancing line may be normal or reactive; assess non-contrast evidence of haemorrhage or injury and compare with pre-operative MRI before calling it residual disease. Use “unclear” when imaging is inadequate or the cavity cannot be interpreted reliably. Some cases need repeat imaging in 2-4 weeks with additional sequences, improved resolution and further planes.

document_sections.heading: 6.6 Definitions for neuroradiological response evaluation
document_sections.content: This section specifies which lesions can be measured reliably and defines imaging response categories.

document_sections.heading: 6.6.1 Measurable tumours
document_sections.content: A lesion is measurable when it can be followed reliably despite small differences in scan planes. The definition reflects historical 2D measurement practice and is mainly based on RANO criteria; it assumes continued widespread use of 2D sequences and may change as volumetric imaging becomes sufficiently reliable and universally available.

document_sections.heading: Measurable lesion
document_sections.content: A measurable lesion is visible in the 3 standard planes and has diameter ≥ 10mm in each when 2D slice thickness plus gap is ≤ 5mm. If thickness plus gap is >5mm, its maximum diameter must be ≥ 2 times that combined thickness and gap. Poorly marginated lesions are non-measurable. With multiple lesions, use the summed volumes of the 5 largest.

document_sections.heading: 6.6.2 Response criteria
document_sections.content: CR requires no detectable residual or recurrent tumour and no meningeal dissemination. PR requires tumour-volume reduction ≥ 50% against the previous staging MRI; for meningeal dissemination, whose extent is only estimable, it denotes considerable reduction. SD spans tumour-volume decrease ≤ 50% through increase ≤ 25% versus the previous staging MRI, without significant change in meningeal dissemination. Some trials use MR for a volume decrease from 50% to 25%. PD denotes volume increase ≥ 25% or a new lesion. For measurable tumours, reliable response assessment may require comparing the best current sequence with its equivalent on the prior or baseline scan. Radiotherapy can cause a radiation reaction with apparent growth. Combined chemotherapy and radiotherapy may produce temporary enlargement of enhancement or FLAIR/T2 abnormality in up to 30-40% of cases, termed pseudo-progression. New enhancement or increased residual size within the radiation field during the first 12 weeks after irradiation must not be deemed true progression unless histology or a short-interval scan after at least 4-6 weeks confirms it. If subsequent MRI confirms growth, date progression to its first documented appearance.

document_sections.heading: 6.7 Multi-Modal Advanced MRI
document_sections.content: Advanced MRI methods can supplement conventional imaging and are most appropriately considered together. The proposed protocols balance acquisition time, quality and implementation across scanners. MRS and DTI are established across childhood, whereas contrast-injection perfusion is less established in children. Dynamic Susceptibility Contrast (DSC) – MRI is currently recommended, although injection details remain under development. Further experience, particularly comparison with DSC-MRI in childhood brain tumours, is needed before proposing an international Arterial Spin Labelling protocol. Other techniques of interest include multi-b value DWI with the IVIM model, MRS imaging of tumour heterogeneity, and steady-state fMRI assessment of functional connectivity, especially in diencephalic syndrome; limited-centre studies are sought. The multimodal protocol table provides acquisition parameters.

document_sections.heading: Data Saving
document_sections.content: Save imaging data in a form suitable for quantitative analysis. DICOM headers should remain interpretable, including after transfer to PACS systems or anonymisation.

document_sections.heading: Contrast Injection
document_sections.content: For DSC-MRI, contrast, usually Gd-DTPA or Gd-DOTA, should be administered by pump injector. As many centres do not inject through central venous lines, an intravenous cannula should be inserted before scanning. To lessen T1 effects, a pre-bolus of 0.05mmol/Kg Gd is recommended at least 2 minutes before another 0.05mmol/Kg Gd, for a total of 0.1mmol/Kg Gd. Standard injection speed is 3ml/sec. The approach has worked in infants, although the pump can be problematic in very small infants and the protocol remains under development for this age group.

document_sections.heading: 6.8 PET Imaging
document_sections.content: Evidence and interest in paediatric brain-tumour PET at diagnosis or during surveillance are growing. PET can supplement MRI with amino-acid tracers O(2-[18F]fluoroethyl-L-tyrosine (FET), L-[methyl- 11C]methionine (MET), or 3,4-dihydroxy-6-[18F]fluoro-Lphenylalamine (FDOPA). 2-deoxy-2-[18F]fluoro-D-glucose (FDG) is less useful because normal grey matter takes it up strongly. Fasting for Four hours before injection is recommended to stabilize metabolic conditions, and a head holder is recommended to limit motion. The tracer table gives doses, scan intervals, reference tissues, tumour-to-background ratios and sites of physiological uptake. Use iterative reconstruction or filtered back projection, with correction for attenuation, scatter, randoms, dead time and decay. Point-spreadfunction reconstruction can introduce artefacts and is not recommended. Recommended voxel size is < 3mm in every direction and spatial resolution is < 6 mm FWHM. Co-register PET with a recent MRI, ideally < 2 weeks old, preferably contrast-enhanced T1W or FLAIR; automated registration can err in children. Imaging specialists should jointly integrate PET and MRI. Report maximal tumour-to-backgroundratio (TBRmax) and metabolically active volume; for DOPA PET, also report maximal tumour-to-normalstriatum ratio (TSRmax). Inflammation and recent seizures can increase tracer uptake. Dynamic FET time-activity curves may be compared with healthy brain; increasing, decreasing or plateau patterns may help distinguish inflammation from tumour.

document_sections.heading: 1. Background and rationale
document_sections.content: Brain tumours account for approximately 25% of paediatric cancers and are childhood and adolescence's most frequent solid tumours. Their clinical and biological diversity accompanies the highest mortality and morbidity among paediatric cancers; care and survival vary substantially across Europe. Neurosurgery contributes to multidisciplinary care through hydrocephalus treatment, complete or partial primary or recurrent tumour resection, biopsy to guide medical care, or combinations at different stages. Acute emergency presentation is common. Expertise, equipment and clinical support in paediatric neurosurgery are important in both urgent and non-acute care. Provision differs across Europe, and the SIOP brain tumour group and European Reference Network aim to reduce variation and support common standards. This chapter sets out paediatric neurosurgical best practice.

document_sections.heading: 2. Paediatric neurosurgical opinion in Europe
document_sections.content: An online survey circulated between October and November 2017 contained 55 questions about European structures, facilities and opportunities for collaboration; it received 388 responses from 44 countries. A subsequent survey of paediatric neurosurgeons associated with SIOP BTG or attending the ESPN meeting in Bonn in 2018 received thirty responses. Just over two thirds said paediatric procedures made up 76 to 100% of their practice; none reported below 25%. Among respondents, 38% worked in institutions treating over 50 paediatric brain-tumour patients yearly, while almost 60% worked in institutions treating 21 to 50. Almost 45% saw up to 15 new cases annually at their centre, and 10% saw more than 50. In this survey, 100% regarded a multidisciplinary team, paediatric intensive care, neuroendoscopy and an operating microscope as mandatory. A yearly minimum case number was considered judicious by 79%; suggested thresholds were thirty or more by 37%, at least twenty by 26%, and at least ten by another 26%. Expert referral centres were favoured by 61%, while 39% considered review-panel consultation sufficient. Over 75% favoured a panel or referral centre for craniopharyngioma, pineal and third-ventricle tumours, optic pathway–hypothalamic and brainstem tumours, and tumours in children under one year of age. The figures and table display the survey responses.

document_sections.heading: 3. Paediatric neurosurgical volume, patient numbers and outcomes
document_sections.content: The effect of provider caseload on paediatric neurosurgical outcomes remains unclear, and relevant brain-tumour literature is limited. The largest cited study assessed 4712 paediatric brain-tumour craniotomy admissions between 1988 and 2000 across 329 United States hospitals and 480 surgeons. Its multivariate analysis associated higher hospital volume with significantly lower mortality: odds ratio 0.52 per tenfold caseload increase. Mortality was 2.3% in the lowest-volume quartile (≤4 cases/ year) and 1.4% in the highest (≥21 cases/ year). Unfavourable discharge disposition was significantly less likely with higher-volume hospitals and surgeons, respectively p<0.001 and p=0.004. Its authors observed centralisation during the 12-year period and mortality falling from 2.7% in the first three years to 1.2% in the last four years. That study assessed morbidity only through discharge disposition, not overall oncological outcomes. Another cited study reviewed 732 children with malignant brain tumours, predominantly medulloblastomas and high-grade gliomas, enrolled between 1986 and 1992. Although general neurosurgeons performed most procedures, outcomes were better for paediatric neurosurgeons or ASPN members; these operators were more likely to remove more than 90% of tumour. ASPN members had the lowest reported neurological-complication likelihood, at 18%.

document_sections.heading: 4. Multidisciplinary set up Components of the multidisciplinary team
document_sections.content: Paediatric neurosurgeons need a supporting multidisciplinary environment that generally includes paediatric neuro-oncologists, neuroradiologists, radiotherapists, pathologists, paediatric neurologists, endocrinologists, rehabilitation professionals, physiotherapists, occupational therapists and social workers. All cases require regular, timely discussion at presentation, diagnosis, after surgery, during adjuvant therapy and at recurrence; the group should formulate the neurosurgical plan. Spinal surgical expertise is also needed for spinal tumours, especially when deformity of a growing spine is present or possible. Meetings should be sufficiently frequent, with scheduled review of team functioning, outcomes, adverse events and complications.

document_sections.heading: Neuroradiology
document_sections.content: Safe surgery depends on accurate depiction of the tumour and adjacent brain. Consensus imaging guidance supports consistent pre-operative and postoperative acquisition, individual care and inter-unit comparison while identifying essential components feasible for basic care. Early postoperative imaging is important: enhancement may develop even within 72 hours, making the first 48 hours preferable. Quantifying residual disease informs adjuvant-treatment decisions, particularly in ependymoma and medulloblastoma. Oxidized methylcellulose (Surgicel) can cause early enhancement and should be avoided during paediatric brain-tumour surgery. Decisions about further surgery, particularly at recurrence, require reproducible imaging of growth; RAPNO has published tumour-specific recommendations. Interventional radiology can support surgery for large vascular tumours in infants and small children. For choroid plexus papillomas and carcinomas, where complete removal improves prognosis, pre-operative embolization can reduce vascularity, change consistency, facilitate complete removal and improve procedural safety.

document_sections.heading: Neuropathology
document_sections.content: WHO classification revisions reflect molecular, genetic and epigenetic findings and clinically relevant differences among subgroups. Neurosurgeons therefore need close neuropathology collaboration and access to advanced molecular diagnostics, even if provided by an external laboratory. An expert review emphasizes obtaining pathological, genetic and biological characterization before postoperative adjuvant therapy. Surgery should collect enough biological material as well as pursue safe resection. Because tumours can be molecularly heterogeneous, sample multiple regions, particularly in medulloblastoma. For open surgery, obtain at least 1 x 1.5 cm3 or 3 x 0.5cm3 specimens. Tissue-processing arrangements from operating room to laboratory should function seven days a week because procedures may be urgent. Molecularly tailored treatment, including MEK pathway inhibitors for some low-grade gliomas, has increased the need to biopsy lesions previously managed on imaging alone, such as optic pathway gliomas. A multicentre molecular discussion group can assist smaller teams. Research tissue is required for some trials, including BIOMEDE, INFORM and SIOPE-PNET5-MB. Outside a trial, research collection and storage require specific consent and ethical approval. Biobanking is not universally available, transfers are governed by agreements, and collaboration across centres and countries is encouraged.

document_sections.heading: 5. Access to neurosurgical equipment
document_sections.content: Paediatric brain-tumour neurosurgery requires an experienced surgeon and equipped operating room. An operating microscope is essential for brain and spinal tumour resection, alongside other important adjuncts.

document_sections.heading: Frameless image-guidance
document_sections.content: Frameless image-guidance permits virtual planning, selection and positioning of the surgical approach, recognition of tumour boundaries, assistance with maximal removal and planned-trajectory burr-hole biopsy of deep lesions. Brain shift after CSF loss, entry of air or progressive resection reduces accuracy; guidance is more accurate near fixed anatomy such as the skull base or falx. Despite those limits, it is considered essential for most brain-tumour resections, especially deep or supratentorial lesions and those in eloquent tissue.

document_sections.heading: Frame-based stereotactic surgery
document_sections.content: Frame-based stereotaxy retains a role despite frameless navigation, most commonly for brainstem-tumour biopsy. A biopsy is not usually needed in routine practice to diagnose diffuse intrinsic brainstem glioma, but may clarify other brainstem lesions with uncertain imaging diagnoses; stereotactic sampling has been reported safe and effective. Robotic needle biopsy is an emerging, comparably accurate possible alternative that may avoid difficult frame placement in smaller children and additional intraoperative imaging.

document_sections.heading: Intra-operative ultrasound
document_sections.content: Intra-operative ultrasound provides repeatable real-time imaging without equipment as costly as intra-operative MRI. It cannot by itself establish complete removal with certainty, but can help exclude an inadvertently retained large tumour component. Newer approaches improve brain and spine visualization and can integrate the probe with frameless navigation.

document_sections.heading: Neuro-endoscopy
document_sections.content: Neuro-endoscopy is essential as an adjunct for brain-tumour care, permitting biopsy of intra- or paraventricular lesions and treatment of associated hydrocephalus. For a pineal tumour with negative markers, endoscopic biopsy through a frontal burr hole can determine whether resection is needed. Germinoma does not require further surgery, whereas confirmed astrocytoma or embryonal tumour requires formal resection. Associated obstructive hydrocephalus can be treated during the same procedure by endoscopic third ventriculostomy.

document_sections.heading: Intra-operative MRI
document_sections.content: Intra-operative MRI combines navigation with real-time imaging and can confirm intended resection, correct for brain shift and reassess residual tumour against eloquent structures. Its principal drawbacks are time and cost. Some hospitals partly address these through a two-room arrangement in which an adjacent scanner operates independently until the patient is transferred during surgery without closing the head.

document_sections.heading: Intra-operative neuro-monitoring
document_sections.content: Monitoring cerebral cortex, tracts and cranial or peripheral nerves supports tailored resection while preserving function. It is commonly used for spinal-cord tumours and lesions involving or near motor or sensory cortex, corticospinal tracts, cranial nerves, brainstem or cauda equina. Approaches include motor and sensory evoked potentials, cortico-bulbar pathways, brainstem auditory evoked potentials and the D wave for motor integrity across an operated spinal segment. Direct stimulation can map relevant structures, particularly for eloquent cortical and brainstem lesions. Cranial-nerve monitoring and direct stimulation significantly improve the safety of resecting posterior fossa ependymoma involving the cerebellopontine angle.

document_sections.heading: 6. Other requirements Paediatric anaesthesia and intensive care
document_sections.content: Specialist paediatric anaesthesia and access to paediatric intensive care are essential for brain-tumour surgery. Expertise is especially important, though not exclusively, for small children with large vascular tumours, because bleeding, rapid fluid shifts and coagulopathy can develop quickly.

document_sections.heading: Definition of high-risk cases and ability to collaborate
document_sections.content: Complex or rare cases include tumours in infants, craniopharyngiomas, pineal tumours, ependymomas and certain recurrent tumours. Wider-network discussion and future virtual tumour boards may help, particularly in smaller countries. SIOP Ependymoma II uses multidisciplinary national panels to assess possible second-look surgery for residual disease. Comparable United Kingdom initiatives for paediatric ependymoma and hypothalamic-pituitary tumours were well received, although clear published evidence of consistent benefit is lacking.

document_sections.heading: Participation in research networks
document_sections.content: Paediatric neuro-oncology units seek research-network collaboration. Given the complexity, rarity and poor prognosis of many tumours, recruitment of as many eligible children as possible into multicentre trials would permit treatment algorithms to be evaluated within a reasonable time. Trial-based investigation and treatment pathways may reduce variation, attract resources and encourage best practice.

document_sections.heading: Information management, discussion of complications
document_sections.content: A paediatric neurosurgical service needs records of procedures, adverse events and complications. Open review and structured evaluation of significant events support learning and continuing improvement. Surgical and postoperative forms facilitate complete, accurate and contemporaneous data capture.

document_sections.heading: Late effects clinic, rehabilitation, neuropsychology support
document_sections.content: The service also requires access to late-effects assessment of surgery alongside chemotherapy and radiotherapy effects. Rehabilitation and neuropsychological support help children and their families pursue the best achievable outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 6. Conclusion
document_sections.content: Paediatric neurosurgery is central to neuro-oncology. Despite unavoidable differences in caseload and resources across Europe, essential components of safe surgical care remain. Collaboration within and between countries can support quality, align pathways and spread best practice.

document_sections.heading: 1. Background Role in paediatric oncology
document_sections.content: Combining histological and molecular analyses is fundamental to accurate diagnosis and appropriate treatment. Studies show morphology alone cannot reliably distinguish histologically similar tumours with very different biology and clinical behaviour. Molecular identification of prognostic or predictive subtypes is especially important for posterior fossa ependymoma, medulloblastoma and histological high-grade glioma; some tumours in the latter category prove biologically low-grade. The WHO classification 2021 introduced new paediatric tumour types and subtypes and made molecular analysis essential for a WHO-conform diagnosis in most entities. Table 1 presents the paediatric CNS tumour categories and molecularly defined entities. Comprehensive assessment, including DNA methylation analysis for most types, is needed. Although immunohistochemical surrogates exist, methylation profiling has the highest accuracy for tumour differentiation and is the WHO-preferred epigenetic method in many cases, especially when diagnosis otherwise remains unresolved. Some entities require detection of characteristic single nucleotide variants, small insertions or deletions, or rearrangements such as fusions and internal tandem duplications for an integrated diagnosis. Because changes including BRAF and FGFR1 mutations or NTRK-fusions can occur across tumour types, and H3F3A and BRAF mutations can coexist, a single alteration may not settle the diagnosis. Comprehensive analysis typically combines methylation profiling for classification and copy-number alterations, DNA sequencing of a brain-tumour gene panel, and RNA fusion sequencing for selected entities. Testing tumour and germline mutations with the same approach is desirable: at least 10% of childhood brain-tumour patients carry pathogenic germline variants in cancer-related genes. Add “NOS” when incomplete testing or limited material prevents full characterization; use “NEC” when comprehensive results do not match an established WHO type.

document_sections.heading: Table 1: WHO classification of paediatric CNS tumours
document_sections.content: The remaining portion of the table presents WHO classification categories for paediatric CNS embryonal tumours, pineal region tumours, melanocytic tumours and sellar region tumours, including molecularly and histologically defined medulloblastomas. It identifies selected entities as new.

document_sections.heading: 1. Background Role in paediatric oncology
document_sections.content: Accurate integrated diagnoses require extensive molecular investigation, including DNA methylation analysis for most tumour types. Although some immunohistochemical markers can serve as substitutes, DNA methylation profiling identifies tumour differentiation most accurately; the WHO classification therefore favours epigenetic analysis for most cases, particularly when other methods cannot resolve the diagnosis. Certain tumour types require detection of characteristic single nucleotide variants, small insertions or deletions, or gene rearrangements for a WHO-integrated diagnosis. An isolated alteration may not settle the diagnosis because BRAF and FGFR1 mutations and NTRK-fusions occur across tumour types, while H3F3A and BRAF mutations can coexist. A comprehensive assessment commonly combines DNA methylation profiling for classification and copy-number alterations, a brain-tumour gene panel using DNA sequencing, and RNA sequencing for fusion detection in selected types. Testing both tumour and germline mutations by the same approach is desirable: at least 10% of children with brain tumours carry pathogenic germline variants in cancer-related genes. When necessary testing is incomplete because an assay or sufficient material is unavailable, the most specific supportable diagnosis receives the designation NOS. When comprehensive testing has been completed but the findings match no established WHO tumour type, the designation is NEC.

document_sections.heading: 2. Institutional requirements
document_sections.content: In most European countries, neuropathology lacks separate, formally regulated certification, so physician and laboratory specialization varies; this does not prevent regions without dedicated neuropathologists from delivering high-quality care. Coordinated neurosurgical and neuropathological processes should permit intraoperative frozen-section assessment, preferably with touch and smear preparations, and secure high-quality samples. Both formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue and frozen tissue should be archived for every paediatric neuro-oncology patient. Required access encompasses basic histology, quality-controlled immunohistochemistry for common WHO markers, DNA methylation analysis and NGS of tumour and blood; FISH and MLPA can serve as surrogate methods.

document_sections.heading: 3. Essential quality parameters
document_sections.content: Paediatric brain tumour submissions for histopathological and molecular assessment are usually uncommon outside specialist centres. Regular scientific exchange and recognition of the limits of histological platforms are mandatory, particularly because European quality-assurance measures have not been established. Typically, at least two experienced neuropathology specialists with > 5 years practise should have full access to histology and immunohistochemistry, alongside local or established referral access to DNA methylation and gene-panel sequencing.

document_sections.heading: 5. Summary
document_sections.content: The essential neuropathology capabilities are conventional histopathology with immunostaining, DNA methylation analysis and gene-panel sequencing of tumour and blood; FISH/MLPA may supplement conventional work-up. RNA sequencing, whole-exome or whole-genome sequencing, and proteomics are desirable. The summary advises preventing NOS diagnoses.

document_sections.heading: 1. Background
document_sections.content: Radiotherapy forms part of multidisciplinary paediatric brain tumour care. For children aged less than 12-36 months, it may be postponed to reduce long-term harm, especially neurocognitive dysfunction. Indications depend broadly on age and tumour histology, with tumour-specific details addressed elsewhere. For Low-grade glioma (LGG), radiotherapy is indicated when disease progresses after surgery or surgery is infeasible; it is indicated for all children with high-grade glioma. All patients with medulloblastoma aged more 3-5 years should be considered for craniospinal radiotherapy. Radiotherapy after resection should be considered for all patients with ependymoma aged >12 months. All germ cell tumour patients except those with completely resected pure mature teratomas require radiotherapy within multimodal treatment. Postoperative treatment for craniopharyngioma is considered according to individual risk. Radiotherapy principles for rare embryonal tumours and ATRT generally follow those for medulloblastoma; for Choroid plexus tumours (CPT), the indication varies by subtype and extent of resection. Many countries are adopting proton beam therapy (PBT), particularly for children with a good prospect of cure. PBT could lessen adverse effects, especially late radiation effects, but conclusive evidence from large prospective studies remains scarce. Its availability should nevertheless be discussed for each child in a multidisciplinary setting, and prospective efficacy and toxicity outcomes after PBT are encouraged through national or international protocols.

document_sections.heading: 2. Institutional requirements
document_sections.content: Paediatric radiotherapy planning, delivery and subsequent care are complex. A treatment centre should have at least two clinical oncologists and dedicated preparation and treatment personnel, including mould-room staff, play specialists, nurses, anaesthetic staff, physicists, a dosimetrist and therapeutic radiographers; wider support should include a paediatric psychologist and psychotherapist. Every patient needing radiotherapy should be discussed by a specialized paediatric multidisciplinary team whose core includes a clinical/radiation oncologist, paediatric oncologist, paediatric specialist nurses and a play therapist. Initial consultations should occur with the radiotherapy team in an age-appropriate outpatient setting. General radiotherapy departments should use designated machines in a child-friendly environment. Patients should be reviewed regularly during treatment to provide support and manage side effects, and established late-effects clinics should proactively address later sequelae.

document_sections.heading: 3. Essential quality parameters
document_sections.content: Centres need a defined pathway identifying the appropriate radiotherapy approach for each patient, including referral outside the hospital for particle beam therapy. Treatment should use an appropriate advanced technique consistent with national guidance or trial protocols. Departments should have externally validated quality assurance, multidisciplinary planning by clinical oncologists, radiographers and physicists, and established checks of daily-treatment accuracy and reproducibility using modern imaging.

document_sections.heading: 5. Summary
document_sections.content: Highly conformal radiotherapy is required for patients treated with curative intent. Selected patients should be referred for proton beam or particle beam therapy in accordance with national clinical guidelines. Every centre should have quality assurance that includes peer review of treatment volumes and plans, plus at least two clinical/radiation oncologists specializing in paediatric radiotherapy. Having at least two such oncologists with appropriate site specialization is desirable. Curative or palliative radiotherapy should not be delivered by an oncologist without a particular interest or experience in paediatric radiotherapy.

document_sections.heading: 1. Background
document_sections.content: Expected 5-year overall survival for children with CNS tumours is currently 73%. Tumour mass effects and neurosurgery, cranial radiotherapy or chemotherapy can produce serious adverse effects, leaving many survivors with lifelong health challenges. Hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction can substantially affect long-term health and wellbeing. Chemotherapy or irradiation of the thyroid or gonads can also cause peripheral endocrine dysfunction. Because endocrine health supports recovery, development, growth and everyday participation, a paediatric endocrinologist should belong to the multidisciplinary neuro-oncology team.

document_sections.heading: Anterior pituitary dysfunction
document_sections.content: Children with sellar or suprasellar tumours can have hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction at diagnosis. Dysfunction can also emerge years after treatment when the tumour did not compress the pituitary region; after radiotherapy, it may begin in the 1st year and become more prevalent with time. This chapter addresses surveillance after brain tumour treatment but excludes craniopharyngioma. In the St. Jude Lifetime Cohort analysis, 51.4% of adult survivors of any childhood cancer who received cranial RT had at least one anterior pituitary disorder after 27.3 years of follow-up. In a nationwide Dutch study of 718 childhood brain tumour survivors, 22.1% developed at least one endocrine disorder within the first 5 years after diagnosis, with most first appearing at a median follow-up of 2.2 years. Younger diagnostic age, hydrocephalus, suprasellar or infratentorial location, and radiotherapy were independent risk factors. RT doses exceeding 30 Gy especially increased hypothalamic-pituitary risk. GH deficiency was the earliest and most common anterior pituitary deficit, affecting up to 22.2 % of patients. A study of 3141 CCS with median follow-up of 24.1 years reported GH, TSH, LH/FSH and ACTH deficiencies in 22.2%, 5.5%, 5.1%, and 4.1%, respectively. Among participants given HP radiotherapy, estimated prevalences were 40.2% for GHD, 11.1% for TSHD, 10.6% for LH/FSHD, 3.2% for ACTHD, and 0.9% for CPP (n = 1089). In another cohort excluding craniopharyngioma and followed for 6.6 years, growth hormone deficiency affected 12.5%, precocious puberty 12.2%, TSH deficiency 9.2%, ACTH deficiency 4.3 %, and LH/FSH deficiency 4.2 %. The figure depicts cumulative endocrine outcomes in a Dutch cohort of 718 survivors excluding craniopharyngioma.

document_sections.heading: Weight gain and obesity
document_sections.content: Brain tumour survivors face an increased risk of obesity, which in childhood raises later risks of diabetes mellitus and cardiovascular disease and warrants attention during follow-up. In a nationwide cohort of 661 survivors, 33.1% experienced significant weight gain, overweight or obesity after median follow-up of 7.3 years. BMI SDS at diagnosis, low-grade glioma, diabetes insipidus and central precocious puberty were associated with these weight outcomes. Other hypothalamic-pituitary deficits were more prevalent in overweight or obese survivors than in those of normal weight. The figure compares endocrine-disorder prevalence by weight group, including normal-weight survivors (n = 457) and overweight or obese survivors (n = 190).

document_sections.heading: Posterior pituitary deficiency
document_sections.content: Central diabetes insipidus (CDI) results from insufficient posterior-pituitary secretion of anti-diuretic hormone (ADH). It can follow tumour-related or surgical injury to the hypothalamus, pituitary stalk or gland, but does not arise as a late effect of radiotherapy. Management requires an experienced paediatric endocrinologist and is generally effective with oral desmopressin. Rarely, disturbed thirst regulation or concurrent ACTH deficiency complicates care, particularly after hypothalamic damage associated with low grade glioma or craniopharyngioma. These cases require regular plasma-sodium and fluid-intake monitoring.

document_sections.heading: 2. Risk factors and time of onset
document_sections.content: The principal risk factors for hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction after treatment of a childhood brain tumour are cranial radiotherapy exposure, sellar or suprasellar tumour location, and hydrocephalus.

document_sections.heading: Cranial radiotherapy.
document_sections.content: Irradiation of the HP region is associated with increased GHD risk. TBI has been linked to GHD but not to TSHD, ACTHD, LH/FSHD or CPP. Higher RT doses and younger age at irradiation increase hypothalamic-pituitary risk. CPP may precede LH/FSHD; pubertal progression requires close monitoring after GnRH analogues are stopped.

document_sections.heading: Cranio-spinal radiotherapy
document_sections.content: Cranio-spinal radiotherapy increases hypothalamic-pituitary risk similarly to cranial irradiation alone. Because the thyroid is usually within the treated field, primary hypothyroidism, thyroid nodules and thyroid carcinoma are additional risks. Combined primary and central hypothyroidism often presents with falling FT4 and mildly elevated TSH. Spinal irradiation can limit trunk growth and standing height despite adequate GH and sex-hormone replacement, particularly during puberty when spinal growth contributes substantially; sitting height should therefore be monitored alongside standing height.

document_sections.heading: Hydrocephalus
document_sections.content: Hydrocephalus has been associated with greater GH-deficiency risk and can also trigger central precocious puberty in young children.

document_sections.heading: Chemotherapy
document_sections.content: Evidence does not show that chemotherapy increases hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction risk. During treatment, however, effects on rapidly dividing growth-plate cells may temporarily limit height gain despite adequate GH production, consistent with transient GH resistance. Alkylating chemotherapy can cause gonadal failure and delayed or arrested puberty.

document_sections.heading: Time of onset.
document_sections.content: After radiotherapy, reported hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction began as early as 0.1 years for GH deficiency and could continue to emerge > 10 years after diagnosis for GH, TSH, ACTH and LH/FSH deficiencies. In children with medulloblastoma treated with 54 Gy, dysfunction most often arose in the 1st 3 years after radiotherapy, and > 80 % had dysfunction after 5 years of follow-up. Average latency was shorter with higher radiation doses.

document_sections.heading: 3. Surveillance
document_sections.content: Surveillance schemes for hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction have been issued by the COG, Dutch Childhood Oncology Group, UK Children’s Cancer Study Group Late Effects Group and Scottish Group. The International Guideline Harmonization Group (IGHG) is developing a harmonized recommendation.

document_sections.heading: Hypothalamic-pituitary function screening
document_sections.content: The chapter proposes follow-up for hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction after brain tumour treatment. Children with a sellar or suprasellar tumour, or dysfunction already present at diagnosis, should be referred directly to a paediatric endocrinologist. The accompanying table sets out radiotherapy-related endocrine late effects, risk factors and surveillance actions. It includes yearly BMI and thyroid assessments where indicated; Tanner-stage and growth-velocity assessments every 6 months for relevant pubertal risks; yearly 08:00 AM morning cortisol for ACTH-deficiency risk; growth measurements every 6 months; and endocrine referral for specified abnormal findings. Its risk and referral thresholds include age < 4 years, radiation dose > 20 Gy, BMI > + 2 SD, pituitary-region dose > 18 Gy or > 40 Gy depending on the outcome, FT4 below the reference interval on 2 separate occasions or a decline > 20 % after starting GH, and cervical irradiation > 20 Gy.

document_sections.heading: Thyroid function screening
document_sections.content: Children whose neck was irradiated during craniospinal treatment should receive yearly TSH and FT4 testing and neck palpation. Thyroid ultrasound may be considered to look for nodules or cancer. The IGHG published thyroid-cancer surveillance recommendations in 2018. Earlier detection of DTC might reduce the extent of surgery or additional radioiodine therapy and possibly reduce morbidity and recurrence; a negative assessment may reassure an at-risk patient. Benefits of earlier treatment remain uncertain because most DTC is curable. False-positive findings can prompt repeated ultrasound or FNA biopsy, causing anxiety, inconvenience, costs and complications of unnecessary procedures. Surveillance may also detect indolent disease that would not have caused clinical problems, leading to overtreatment; false negatives may provide misplaced reassurance. The IGHG therefore recommends discussing surveillance frequency and choice of neck palpation or ultrasound with patients and parents according to individual needs.

document_sections.heading: Gonadal function screening
document_sections.content: Survivors treated with gonadotoxic therapies such as alkylating agents have the highest risk of ovarian or testicular failure, although even agents regarded as low-risk may affect fertility. IGHG guidance addresses long-term surveillance for both sexes. For female survivors exposed to alkylating agents or radiotherapy involving the ovaries or hypothalamic-pituitary region, monitoring of growth, pubertal development and yearly LH/FSH/estradiol is recommended because these exposures increase POI risk. In males, gonadotoxic treatment can impair spermatogenesis and cause testosterone deficiency or sexual dysfunction. Counselling about these risks is recommended after alkylating agents or irradiation involving the hypothalamic-pituitary region or potential old spinal fields. At-risk prepubertal and peripubertal males should have growth and Tanner-stage progression monitored for testosterone deficiency. In postpubertal males, early-morning total serum testosterone measurement at clinically appropriate intervals is reasonable. Sperm, oocyte or ovarian-tissue cryopreservation should be considered, ideally before gonadotoxic treatment.

document_sections.heading: Indications for referral
document_sections.content: A paediatric endocrinologist should preferably participate in every child's brain tumour multidisciplinary team to support early identification and treatment of hypothalamic-pituitary deficits. Children with tumours affecting the hypothalamic-pituitary region should be referred at diagnosis for individualized monitoring and treatment when needed. Referral is also indicated for slowing growth, absent pubertal progression, abnormal laboratory findings or a history suggestive of pituitary deficiency.

document_sections.heading: 4. GH treatment in childhood brain tumour survivors
document_sections.content: GH deficiency is frequent after cranial irradiation and can compromise final height; an adequate GH state also supports metabolic health, bone health and muscle strength. Large cohort studies found no increased recurrence of the original tumour or secondary-tumour risk among CCS treated with GH compared with those not treated with GH. Prospective studies are still needed to confirm safety, determine when to start GH after complete remission, address children with persistent low-grade glioma and GHD, and establish optimal dosing. Most current recommendations advise that GH can be given safely after GH deficiency is established. Recent guidelines suggest waiting until patients have been disease free for at least one year, but this rests on little evidence. For children who may never become disease free, such as some with low grade glioma, the paediatric endocrinologist, oncologist, patient and parents must discuss individual potential benefits and harms.

document_sections.heading: 1. Background
document_sections.content: Childhood CNS tumours can disrupt visual anatomy and development, producing reduced visual acuity (VA), visual field (VF) defects, diplopia and abnormal eye movements. Manifestations depend substantially on tumour location and involvement of afferent visual pathways or the cranial nerves of the efferent system. Obstructive hydrocephalus, brain oedema, leptomeningeal spread or cerebral venous thrombosis can raise intracranial pressure, produce papilledema and further threaten sight. During early visual development, additional deprivation from refractive errors, keratopathy, cataracts or strabismus may cause amblyopia and further loss. Adult survivors have increased long-term risks of unilateral or bilateral blindness (RR 14.8), cataracts (RR = 11.9) and diplopia (RR 8.8), with potential effects on cognition, independence, driving and education. Large tertiary-centre series reported that less than 50% of newly diagnosed children received baseline ophthalmological referral, at a median of 9 months (range 0-94 months) after diagnosis. Acute illness and prioritization of lifesaving care can delay assessment; visual symptoms may also be underreported, especially in infants, young children and those with VF defects. Standardized assessment and follow-up recommendations aim to improve detection and enable earlier intervention that might prevent or lessen irreversible visual loss.

document_sections.heading: 2. Tumour Location and Specific Manifestations
document_sections.content: Compression or infiltration of visual pathways or visual-system cranial nerves produces manifestations that vary chiefly with CNS tumour location. The location-based symptom table summarizes the principal visual findings.

document_sections.heading: Posterior Fossa (PF)
document_sections.content: PF tumours are the most common CNS neoplasms of childhood and affect sight through several mechanisms. Raised intracranial pressure commonly causes acute papilledema in the vast majority of children with PF masses. Papilledema usually resolves when the pressure is adequately treated, but severe or prolonged pressure can lead to optic atrophy, axonal death and visual loss. In very young children, papilledema can be absent because unfused sutures allow head enlargement. Early papilledema may cause few symptoms apart from an enlarged blind spot; nasal, arcuate or central VF defects can follow. CN-VI palsy from dorsal pontine compression or brainstem displacement may cause esotropia, horizontal diplopia and compensatory head turning. Reported findings in children with PF tumours include gaze palsy and strabismus (42%), upbeat nystagmus (23%) and abnormal acuity (15%), defined as VA below 20/40 (or > 0.3 logMAR) in one or both eyes. Frequent tumour types are WHO grade IV Medulloblastoma (MBL), cerebellar WHO grade I pilocytic astrocytoma (PA), and ependymoma (EP); MBL and EP carry greater abnormal-vision risk than cerebellar PA. Survivors of MB or cerebellar PA frequently have persistent strabismus (25-29%) or nystagmus (12.5- 18%). ATRT and rare embryonal tumours can occur here with similar features.

document_sections.heading: Supratentorial Region
document_sections.content: Temporal, parietal and occipital tumours present with visual symptoms less often than midline or PF lesions. Occipital or temporal tumours affecting visual cortex, geniculate bodies or optic radiations may nevertheless cause VF defects, including homonymous hemianopia. Possible histologies include high grade glioma (HGG), ependymoma, LGG, embryonal tumours and other rare entities.

document_sections.heading: Visual Pathways
document_sections.content: Visual dysfunction is often the main or only manifestation of a tumour infiltrating visual pathways. Optic pathway gliomas (OPG) are mostly histologically low-grade glioma (LGG), but may remain indolent or progress repeatedly and cause severe visual sequelae. A substantial proportion of affected children experience impairment, and 5 - 10% meet legal-blindness criteria. Uni- or bilateral VA and VF defects vary with lesion position; homonymous and bitemporal hemianopia are frequent. Children below 1 year of age and those with post-chiasmatic OPG appear more likely to experience VA deterioration. Approximately 15% of children with Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) have OPG. Its course is indolent in up to 70 - 85%, while about 15% - 30% develop more aggressive behaviour and visual deficits. Isolated optic nerve gliomas (IONG), whether or not associated with NF1, may cause proptosis and optic pallor or atrophy as well as acuity or field loss. Optic nerve sheaths meningioma, commonly associated with Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2), can present similarly. Large hypothalamic-chiasmatic OPG can obstruct CSF flow, raise intracranial pressure and produce papilledema.

document_sections.heading: Suprasellar (extra-optic)
document_sections.content: Suprasellar tumours outside the visual pathways, including craniopharyngioma (CP), commonly impair vision through compression of the optic chiasm and neighbouring structures. At diagnosis or after treatment, about 30% of children with CP have substantial visual decline and about 10% are legally blind. Manifestations include VA loss (43.9%) and VF defects (38%); uni- (13%) or bitemporal hemianopia (29.5%) are the most frequent field defects. Blindness in one or both eyes has been reported in up to 13%. Fundoscopic alterations occur in 32% in association with suprasellar tumour, obstructive hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure; reported findings include papilledema (25.8%) and optic pallor or atrophy (44.8%). Orthoptic examination may identify strabismus (16.5%), diplopia (14.5%), nystagmus (6%) or cranial nerve defects (13%). Suprasellar intracranial germ cell tumours (iGCT), including germinoma, can produce comparable findings.

document_sections.heading: Brain Stem and Pons
document_sections.content: Brainstem or pontine tumours frequently affect CN-III, CN-IV or CN-VI, causing diplopia, exo-/esotropia, strabismus and other oculomotor deficits; compensatory torticollis can preserve binocular vision. The clinical course varies from aggressive to relatively indolent. An intrinsic pontine lesion with an interval from symptom onset to diagnosis of < 3-6 months is more suggestive of diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) or H3K27M WHO grade IV diffuse midline glioma (DMG). Exophytic dorsal brainstem lesions with a longer symptomatic interval are more suggestive of lower-grade disease.

document_sections.heading: Pineal/ Tectal plate
document_sections.content: Pineal lesions commonly accompany obstructive hydrocephalus and raised intracranial pressure. Reported visual findings include papilledema (69%), optic atrophy (5%) and VF defects (4-5%). Parinaud’s Syndrome comprises impaired upward gaze and convergence with light-near dissociation of the pupillary reflex and is typical of pineal or mesencephalic/tectal lesions. Associated convergence-retraction nystagmus localizes disease to the dorsal midbrain or tectal plate. Pineal neoplasms commonly include WHO grade IV pineoblastoma and secreting or non-secreting germ cell tumours (GCT), whereas tectal or mesencephalic tumours more often have LGG histology.

document_sections.heading: 3. Treatment-related Visual Impairment
document_sections.content: Surgery, chemotherapy (CT), radiation (RT) and targeted treatment for CNS neoplasms may cause acute or long-term visual impairment (VI).

document_sections.heading: Surgery/RICP Treatment
document_sections.content: Resection near the optic chiasm, optic radiations or occipital lobes may cause postoperative VF or VA deficits. Surgery for posterior fossa ependymoma or medulloblastoma can affect CN VI or gaze, causing ocular misalignment or nystagmus. Perioperative optic nerve dissection or abrupt interruption of its blood supply after decompressive shunting and rapid intracranial-pressure changes can cause sudden, often irreversible acuity or field loss.

document_sections.heading: Chemotherapy and Targeted Agents
document_sections.content: Visual complications reported with standard CT agents include optic neuritis, central or peripheral neuropathy, papilledema, maculopathy, cataracts and visual loss. Nitrosureas (CCNU) and platinum compounds (cisplatin) can produce dose-dependent retinal toxicity. Rare reports associate vincristine and methotrexate with possible ptosis, optic neuropathy and, less frequently, posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) and visual loss. Extended steroid treatment can cause cataracts. BRAF inhibitors have been associated with uveitis (41%), dry eyes, conjunctivitis and, rarely, photosensitivity (4%). MEK inhibitors have been associated with retinopathy mainly in adults, ranging from OCT-only intraretinal fluid to retinal vein occlusion (RVO), blurred vision and, rarely, irreversible VA loss. Whether MEK-Retinopathy also occurs in children remains unclear. Regular VA assessment and macular OCT/infrared fundus imaging can help monitor these effects and inform treatment interruption or termination before irreversible loss.

document_sections.heading: Radiotherapy
document_sections.content: RT increases risk of radiation-induced necrosis, retinopathy and amblyopia. Cataract risk is associated with posterior fossa or temporal-lobe radiation doses >30Gy and prolonged steroids, particularly prednisone. A dose of 50Gy or more to the eye significantly raises risks of cataract, diplopia, dry eye and blindness. Among patients receiving ≥50 Gy bilaterally to the chiasm or both optic nerves for suprasellar or anterior visual-pathway tumours, between 5% and 8.5% were at risk of VA decline. Cranio-spinal irradiation (CSI), still routinely used for medulloblastoma and other malignant CNS tumours, is associated with dry eye, retinal opacity and posterior subcapsular cataract, occurring at a median of 27.6 months and in up to 28.8% of children after CSI. Hearing loss, posterior fossa syndrome and neurocognitive deficits may further worsen functional outcomes.

document_sections.heading: 4. Recommended Baseline Visual Assessment -RAFFO
document_sections.content: All children with a newly diagnosed CNS neoplasm are recommended to receive baseline neuro-ophthalmological evaluation, regardless of tumour site. The essential RAFFO parameters are Refraction, Visual Acuity (VA), Visual Fields (VF), Fundoscopic examination and Orthoptic assessment. The associated tables describe parameter definitions and distinguish minimum requirements from best clinical practice.

document_sections.heading: Refraction
document_sections.content: Pre-existing or new refractive errors should be assessed before other visual measures, so a correctable lens problem is not mistaken for VA loss from another cause.

document_sections.heading: Visual Acuity (VA)
document_sections.content:
VA measures visual resolution and remains the most important visual measure for children with CNS tumours. Assess best-corrected VA (BCVA) in each eye, at far and near distances if possible, and report the threshold optotype detail in logMAR, from 0.0 for normal vision to 2.0. A change of 0.2 LogMAR VA or more is clinically relevant. If quantitative measurement is infeasible, fixation observations can help establish whether vision is present; document Hand Motion (HM), counting fingers (CF), Light Perception (LP) or No Light Perception (NLP), as appropriate. Testing depends on age and cooperation: Teller Acuity preferential looking Cards (TAC) are commonly used for infants and preverbal children, whereas Lea symbols, Cardiff Acuity Test, Kays Picture Chart and later HOTV or Snellen charts suit older children.

Changing VA test methods can slightly overestimate or underestimate longitudinal results. Because vision develops rapidly over the first 2-3 years and reaches full potential only after 5 years of age, age-specific normal ranges should be used in young children.

document_sections.heading: Visual Fields (VF)
document_sections.content: An attempt to identify VF deficits is considered essential, even when age or cooperation prevents full measurement. Assess each eye separately where possible, using an age-appropriate method. Confrontation or BEFIE testing is used below 5 years of age; Goldmann kinetic perimetry or preferably automated perimetry (HFA 30-2 sita fast or Octopus) is recommended for older, cooperative children. Report defects as symmetric or asymmetric and specify nasal or temporal restriction from 0° for complete restriction to no restriction. Because VF deficits are often underreported, the document supplies questions for children and parents to help identify them.

document_sections.heading: Fundoscopic exam
document_sections.content: Dilated fundoscopy best evaluates papilledema, optic pallor and atrophy when the child can cooperate. Papilledema can be absent with subacute or chronic raised intracranial pressure; its absence does not rule out a CNS tumour. Early damage may affect peripheral fields, with later VA loss from optic atrophy and axonal loss. OCT may provide a more objective assessment of disc swelling through RNFL thickening when fundoscopy is infeasible or inconsistent.

document_sections.heading: Orthoptic examination and eye movement disorder assessment
document_sections.content: Initial neurological and ideally orthoptist-led examination can evaluate ocular alignment, movements and relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) through assessment of CN III, IV and VI, pupillary responses, cover testing and pursuit. Findings may include intermittent or persistent exotropia or esotropia, nystagmus and gaze palsy. Head turning or torticollis can compensate for abnormal movements and diplopia. Colour or contrast vision testing, slit-lamp examination particularly when NF1 is suspected, and OCT measurements of RNFL or GCL-ILP may be useful in selected cases but are not essential. OCT and RNFL thickness are emerging objective markers, including in OPG. A cut-off of 76 µm has been used to define an abnormal OCT, and a change of ≥10% in circumpapillary RNFL or macular GCL-ILP thickness has been considered significant over time. There is currently no clear consensus linking OCT change to progression or treatment response; interpret it with functional measures and account for measurement subjectivity and artifacts.

document_sections.heading: 5. Recommended Visual Surveillance After Treatment
document_sections.content: Pre-existing or new visual impairment can persist or develop during and after CNS tumour therapy. Regular ophthalmological surveillance is suggested for affected children. Its frequency and duration should reflect tumour location, treatment and the presence, severity and likelihood of further visual dysfunction.

document_sections.heading: 6. Must Have/Desirable/Not To Do Recommendations
document_sections.content: The recommendations table assigns responsibilities and target populations. Required actions include history-taking about visual symptoms and neurological and fundoscopic examination in children with suspected tumours; baseline neuro-ophthalmological referral for every newly diagnosed child; multidisciplinary diagnosis and care when visual signs are present; and referral for visual-impairment rehabilitation. Hand-held OCT and RNFL/GCL surrogate measures are desirable in selected young children, including those with OPG or CP. Baseline assessment must not be omitted or delayed merely because visual symptoms are absent, and ophthalmological follow-up must not be discontinued after CNS tumour treatment.

document_sections.heading: 1. Background
document_sections.content: Quality of survival (QoS) concerns the presence and effects of long-term neurocognitive, endocrine, other medical, behavioural, emotional and adaptive-functional sequelae in CNS tumour survivors. Improving survival makes evaluation and follow-up important for supporting children, adolescents and families. Tumour- and treatment-related factors put this population at high risk of lasting sequelae; among childhood and adolescent cancers, CNS tumours have the highest morbidity and mortality. A biopsychosocial, interdisciplinary approach is recommended at diagnosis and during and after treatment. Neuropsychological surveillance and interventions warrant particular attention because cognitive late effects are common and can impair education, employment, independent living and quality of life.

document_sections.heading: 2. Institutional requirements
document_sections.content: At diagnosis and throughout and after treatment, each patient should have access to neuropsychological assessment under international recommendations; endocrine, ophthalmological and hearing evaluation; inpatient or outpatient neuro-rehabilitation; physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy; AYA transition support; palliative care; vocational, social-work, child-life or teaching support; and age- and risk-adapted fertility preservation before gonadotoxic treatment.

document_sections.heading: 3. Essential quality parameters
document_sections.content: The International Guidelines Harmonization Group for Late Effects of Childhood Cancer develops medical and psychosocial surveillance guidance. Paediatric oncology centres should know this guidance and provide minimum standards for medical, neuropsychological and psychosocial follow-up. Publicly available guidance also comes from the Children's Oncology Group (COG) and PanCare. These guidelines adapt follow-up to exposure to surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy and address multiple care domains.

document_sections.heading: 5. Summary
document_sections.content: Required resources include a qualified multidisciplinary team led by paediatric neuro-oncology with regular meetings, rehabilitation and physiotherapy, occupational and speech therapy, neuropsychological assessment, psychosocial support, guidance for school and family, an acute and long-term rehabilitation plan, AYA transition planning and palliative care. Quality of Survival should be assessed at diagnosis and initial treatment. Standardized neuropsychological evaluation during regular follow-up and a dedicated multidisciplinary follow-up team are desirable. Follow-up should not assess only medical status: psychosocial, neuropsychological and school functioning also need evaluation.
